subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL. COMMITTEE PRESENTED.

speechtext:
Mr. G. B. NICHOLSON (East Algoma) laid on the table of the House the second report of the Special Committee appointed for the purpose of inquiring forthwith as to the prices charged throughout Canada for foodstuffs, clothing, fuel, and other necessaries of life, and as to the rates of profits made thereon by dealers and others concerned in their production, distribution and sale, also as to the rentals of dwelling houses in industrial centres of Canada, and rates of return of capital invested therein, . etc., as follows:
Your Committee since their appointment on the 30th Cay ol May last have held thirty-six morning, afternoon and evening sessions, heard and considered the evidence given under oath of sixty-six persons representing various producers, manufacturers, wholesale, retail and consumers' organizations from various parts of Canada; also have received numerous petitions, resolutions and other communications, all of which have been considered.
Your committee have been engaged almost continuously from the 5th day of June last to the present date in obtaining all information possible from witnesses and all available sdurces, but have not yet reached a point in their investigation that would warrant them in submitting Anal conclusions. There has come to the attention of your committee evidence in regard to undue profits being made on certain commodities. Your committee in order to provide a means by which a recurrence of such may be prevented and chat the public may be protected against unfair practices in trade recommend to the consideration of the House and the Government that legislation be enacted at this session of Parliament creating a tribunal with power to investigate mergers, trust, monopolies or organizations of any kind or nature, which tend to limit facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing, or preventing, limiting or lessening manufacture or production, or fixing a common price, or a resale price, or a common rental, or a common cost of storage, or transportation, or enhancing the price, rental or cost of article, rental, storage or transportation, or preventing ot lessening competition in or substantially controlling within any particular district, or generally, production, manufacture, purchase, barter, sale, transportation, insurance, or supply, or otherwise restraining or injuring commerce or unduly enhancing the price of the necessaries of life, also with regulative power in connection with discriminations In price between different purchaser of commodities, exclusive purchase and sale arrangements, Intercorporate shareholding and inter-locking directorates and unfair methods in commerce.
All of which is respectfully submitted.

subtopic: PROHIBITION.

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of an amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 107, to confirm the Order in Council of the 24th day of February, 1919, and the Order in Council of the 12th day of April, 1919, in amendment thereof.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PROHIBITION.
subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION OF AN AMENDMENT MADE BY THE SENATE TO BILL No. 107.
speechtext:
The Bill in question is entitled: "An Act to Confirm the Order in Council of the 24th day of February, 1919 prohibiting the importation, manufacture and transiportation of intoxicating liquors, and the Order in Council of the 12th day of April, 1919, in amendment thereof." The principal provision of the Bill, apart from certain amendments which it establishes, is as follows:
The Orders in Council marked "A" and "B" in the Schedule to this Act are hereby declared to be valid and are ratified and confirmed, and declared to have the force of law according to their terms.
The principal reason for the introduction of the Bill is to be found in one provision of the Order in Council, which I find on page 6 of the Bill as printed:
These regulations shall be construed as supplementary to the prohibitory laws now m force, or that may be hereafter in force m any province or territory, and shall continue in force during the continuance of the present war, and for twelve months thereafter.
There was some doubt, owing to a difference of opinion on the construction of the War Measures Act of 1914, as to whether or not the concluding portion of this paragraph was operative in law-that is to say, the provision that these regulations should continue in force for twelve months after the war. The Bill was passed by the House of Commons, and it was amended in the Senate by striking out these words and therefore absolutely defeating the only purpose for which the Bill had been introduced into, and passed by, this House. In other words, the Senate struck out the words from the Order in Council:
and for twelve months thereafter.
The net result of that is of the most extraordinary character. It would have been far better, and more direct, if the Senate had simply rejected the Bill altogether, because that would have brought about the precise result which follows from the action they did take. And, if this House should assent to the amendment proposed by the Senate this House would be denying the principle which it affirmed when it passed

this Bill. Therefore, I beg leave to move, seconded by Hon. Mr. Rowell, the following resolution:
This House doth disagree with the Senate Amendment for the following reasons:-
(1) The Senate Amendment destroys the principle and purpose of the Bill. The Orders in Council are valid during the continuance of the war in any event and without any confirming Act; and' possibly they may be valid for the period of twelve months thereafter as mentioned in the Orders in Council. Therefore the

Bill as amended by the Senate does not give the Orders in Council any greater validity than they now possess while on the other hand it expressly limits their possible operation.
(2)	In view of the difficulties which confront the' country during the period of readjustment and having regard to dangers of unemployment and to the conditions of unrest which prevail throughout the Dominion, the reasons which justified the passing of the Orders in Council continue to exist during demobilization and will continue to exist throughout the period covered by the Bill as passed by the House.
(3)	The Bill as passed by the House is in the interests of the maintenance of peace, order and good government in Canada, and it will tend to prevent waste, promote thrift, conserve resources and increase national efficiency.

The figures which I have given rather put in a different light, the remarks of the hon. member the other day as to exorbitant profits and as to the robbery that was being carried out in these elevators. I stated the other day that the Grain Growers had stated to the Board of Grain Commissioners some years ago that if the Board would guarantee them against shortages in their elevator, the board could take all the overages that would arise. But at the same time we said, "if you are going to hold us responsible for the shortages that- may arise in the elevator-and we are responsible for them under the Act-then it is but fair that you should not appropriate all of the surplus? How is the matter to be worked out? For instance, in two years that I recall, we had overages in wheat in our elevator and shortages in oats; would the Government take all the surplus in wheat and hold us responsible for all the shortage in oats? These facts have to be taken into consideration in any treatment of this question.
With respect to screenings, I do not wish to amplify what I stated the other day; but let me restate it briefly. In all cases where the screenings cleaned out of grain amount to over 3 per cent, a separate return is made to the farmer for the value of the screenings and a charge of one-half cent a bushel is made for cleaning. Where the screenings are under 3 per cent, no return is made to the farmer, but no charge is made for cleaning the grain.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the other day I discussed the resolution which preceded this Bill and I drew attention at that 259
time to certain very flagrant abuses, and also to what I characterized as pernicious practices on the part of the terminal elevators at the heads of the lakes in;handiing grain entrusted to their care. During the course of my remarks I pointed out to the House the enormous quantities of overages that occurred in these terminal elevators at each annual weigh-up, and I named a number of elevators.
Among others, I cited the case of the United Grain Growers, or, as it is characterized in the official report of Price, Waterhouse & Company, the Grain Growers Grain Company. This morning the exMinister of Agriculture, the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), undertook to justify these overages. He said that the figures I had given to the House the other day were entirely inaccurate and alleged that I did not know what I iwas talking about. As nearly as parliamentary etiquette -would permit, he,intimated that I had not been truthful in my statements. Without any desire to delay the House unduly I wish to do two things. First, I am going to justify absolutely and beyond any question of doubt the figures I gave the other day, and I shall perhaps amplify them somewhat. Secondly, I must insist upon securing the attention of the minister (Hon. Mr. Maclean) to the danger I *fear, that this Bill will not only perpetuate 'but will actually increase these abuses. These two things I purpose doing in as brief a time as the importance of the subject will allow.
My hon. friend from Marquette attempted to justify these overages. IHe said it was necessary to allow overages in order to offset possible shortage, as any elevator might have a shortage. I shall not argue that point from an: academic standpoint, but I intend to give to the Committee the experience of five years' operation of his own company, and others, as set forth in this report of Price, Waterhouse & Company, who made a careful detailed and special audit of every elevator at the head*of the Lakes. That document, Mr. Chairman, is not only authentic, but it was prepared with the distinct object of showing whether these abuses did occur tor not, and whether the Grain Act as applied and administered was a fair Act-not fair to individual operators, but to the (shipper and to the farmer generally. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Crerar) cast some rather sarcastic remarks in my direction this morning, and he insinuated that I had picked out the Grain Growers Grain

Company especially. I cited the other day the Consolidated Grain Company, the Empire Elevator Company, the Thunder Bay Elevator Company, and one or two others, and at the time I said I had in my hand a list of all the various companies and that they were equally guilty. The hon. gentleman advances the argument that overages are necessary to offset shortage. I think I state his argument fairly. If I am not stating it fairly he can correct me; but I think I repeat his words almost exactly.

That if the elevator company had to carry the liability of shortages-and they have, under the regulations of the Grain Act today-then they should not have all the overages taken from them. On the other hand, if the Government are willing to assume the liability for shortage, I have no objection.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I will take it exactly as the hon. member says. He says that if the Government are going to deprive the elevators of the overages then they should offset the shortages. I am going to show that if the Government took every ounce of overage of the elevators-and I will cite his own elevator as an illustration-the elevators would still have out of screenings a very ample reward and insurance against any possible shortage. I will take his own figures and ask the Committee to follow me, because I do not believe the House really appreciates the significance of this, one-half of one per cent which is allowed in this Bill on overages. I will quote figures to demonstrate beyond the shadow of a doubt that if that clause passes it will be an iniquitous piece of legislation, and I cannot put that too strongly. The Grain Growers' Grain Company in a period of five years had overages of 357.000 bushels.

Those figures, ,added to the ones I have given, are net surplus retained by the elevator after making all accounts to the farmers. The hon. gentleman interjected a remark .that would tend to mislead the House. He says that they must account to the farmer for these things.
I say, Mr. Chairman, on the authority of this report, that it is the practice of all the elevators at the head of the lakes not to account to a farmer, or not to account to a shipper, who consigns his grain to the elevator when there is a dockage, unless the farmer or the shipper directly demands an accounting, and I say further that this is seldom done in practice. Let me give an illustration. I walked out of the House the other night after speaking on this subject and a gentleman came up to me and said: " Stevens, you are absolutely correct; 1 shipped to the Grain Growers' elevator three carloads of wheat; I was docked at the shipping point one per cent, and I was
docked at the elevator four per cent, and it was good wheat, high-class wheat; that meant a dockage in round figures of $300 or $325." I said: " How much did they account to you for?" And how much, Mr. Chairman, do you think it was? The dockage amounted to approximately $325, and he got back a cheque for, I think, $2.50. Certainly the elevator's account, but they account upon their own responsibility, they account upon the practice which is followed, and the figures I have submitted to the House show beyond all peradventure that these dockages and overages are absolutely unjustified on a sound business principle.

Now the question of
whether these overages are legal arises. It has been intimated to the House that these overages) are permissible and that they are correct according to the Act. I will show you that is not so. I am not giving my own figures or my own opinions, but here is section 123 of the Grain Act and it declares as follows:

No person owning, managing, operating, or otherwise interested in any terminal elevator shall buy or sell grain at any point in the Eastern or Western Inspection Division.
And in section 136 we find this provision occurs:
Every terminal warehouse man in the Western Inspection Division shall pay or make allowance to the owner in all domestic grain, of a commercial value in screening.
and so on. My contention is that these clauses show the intention of the Act to be that a clear accounting shall be made. The figures show that no such accounting is made, and these excessive overages and screenings are secured by what I call absolutely fair and unsound-and I go further and say-dishonest business methods.
In connection with the operation of terminal elevators this Parliament in 1912, I remember very well, debated the question at length. It was a question in the opinion of many members whether we should allow any terminal elevators to operate privately or to have them all under the Government. There was a tendency towards Government operation, but in framing this Act we thought we were safeguarding the public and in doing that we made it absolutely illegal-I repeat we made it absolutely illegal-for terminal elevators to engage in the buying and selling of grain. I have quoted you the section referring to that. Now what are the facts? I find, Sir, in looking through this report, that a very considerable amount of dealing in grain occurred by these elevator companies, and in order to be properly seized of the nature of these transactions, we should remember this:	Grain is committed to the elevators
in trust. They are warehouse men, they are storage men, and the farmer and the shipper entrusts his grain to them as I entrust my money-what little I make from-time to time-to a bank, or you entrust your goods to a warehouse in the city; and it is just as iniquitous a practice for a bank to take funds, or a bank teller to take funds, belonging to a customer and use them for his private use, or for a warehouse man having package goods in his warehouse to take them out and deal and trade in them, as it is for the grain elevator men to trade in the grain entrusted to their care at .the head of the Lakes. I say there is no difference in the morality of the cases cited. At any rate we put a provision in the Act for the purpose of safeguarding the public.
It was well known that gambling in grain was a common practice, and my hon. friend who has been taking so much interest in

toy remarks to-day, was .one of the individuals who moved'in the city of Winnipeg a few years, ago. that dealing in options should be made a criminal offence,-that is that not merely dealing in options in the terminal elevators, but dealing in options at all, should be made' a criminal offence. I shall not discuss that but T would remind him that it is certainly clear that in the operation of a terminal elevator, to which 'is entrusted the grain of the shipper, that dealing in options is certainly a wrongful practice. What do we find? We find that a number of elevators., including, the one operated by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crerar) dealt in options. That is, they took the grain belonging to .other people, and sold it, knowing that overages would occur at the end of the year which would make good the shortage of that grain. They dealt in the grain that other people entrusted to their care, contrary to the law. Here are some figures from this report

The Consolidated Elevator Company in 1913-14 lost $2,340 and in 1915-16 lost $30,041. in 1916-17-$1,700 in trading in grain. Total loss, $34,080 in three years. There are other causes, but this is sufficient to demonstrate the point I am driving at, and it is this: if we do not properly safeguard the people's interest there will come a time when these operators will become so bold that they will use this grain recklessly; they will make losses that they cannot offset by overages ; and the first thing you know, Sir, we will have a collapse of elevators at the head of the Lakes with huge scandals, because of the impossibility of their making good the losses of the grain which they

had illegally, contrary to the Grain Act, taken from these elevators.
Now I come to another point. Two or three hon. gentlemen, who spoke on the subject the other day and to-day intimated that the profits on the fees were not sufficient for these elevators. Let us approach that question in an economic and scientific way. What are the functions of these elevators? I have already intimated that they have a quasi-public function to perform-that is to care for, to forward, and to store the grain of the farmers of the Great West. That is what they are there for, and the function which they exercise is a public function. Is it right, Mr. Chairman, that bodies representing a business of that type shall make huge profits? Am I not correct in saying that the operators of elevators of that kind would be making a fair profit at 7.8 per cent, and that if they did so they could not complain very much? Yet they have intimated to the House that the fees are so small they cannot make legitimate earnings. What are those fees? They are as follows, and I am not sure whether they have not been increased :
| cents per bushel for elevating, insurance and 15 days storage.
%o cents per bushel per day or one cent per mopth.
Cleaning l cent per bushel.
Drying 4 cents per bushel wet, and 1J cents for tough.
We find in summing this up that these elevators at the head of the Lakes took, in overages, and in screenings, in the period under survey, five years, about $8,000,000, or to be more exact, between $7,500,000 and $8,000,000. In the years subsequent to this their revenues are on that ratio, or are very much increased, and as near as I can gather them without the detailed figures before me, outside of the five years to which I -have referred, in the last eight years, approximately, $15,000,000 has been wrongfully and illegally appropriated by the elevators at the head of the Lakes.
Now, we might proceed to another phase of this question. The hon. gentleman, this morning, insinuated that I had deceived the House, that I had not been truthful in my statement, in that I stated the other day that the Grain Growers' Grain Company had realized from their elevator at the head of the Lakes, or from the elevator operated by them at that point, 211 per cent, or deducting the loss they made that year gambling in grain which belonged to other people, 187 per cent. He quoted certain figures to prove it. I will quote these figures
and I will explain them, and I defy my hon friend to show wherein I am inaccurate in the slightest degree. Let me apply these figures also to the reasonableness of the fees charged. In the first place, I am going to quote the averages for five years-. I do not want to burden the House any more than is necessary, but for five years the Grain Growers' elevator, or the elevator operated by them, earned out of fees- legitimate, honourable fees-7.73 per cent, or nearly 8 per cent; including screenings. 11.81 per cent, and including overages, 18.85 per cent. The hon. gentleman asked this House if those earnings, were not reasonable. They are not reasonable, but the unreasonableness of them will be drawn to the attention of the House when I point out that these figures are based upon the cost of the elevator. They did not have one single dollar invested in the elevator. The elevator belonged to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and there was not one single dollar of the money of the Grain Growers' Company invested in that elevator. This figure is based, as all the others are, upon the assumption that these profits were earned by a company owning an elevator and making the necessary allowance therefor. What are the facts?
The facts are that the Grain Growers' Grain Company leased an elevator from the Canadian Pacific Railway. According to Price, Waterhouse' and Company, an ample working capital allowance for an- elevator is $50,000 per million bushels capacity, or, in the case of this elevator with a 2,000,000 capacity, $100,000 of working capital. I am absolutely safe in saying that the Grain Growers' Company did not (have invested $100,000 capital in the operation of this elevator. But, we will allow them exactly the same as any of the other elevators to which I shall refer in a moment. The earnings of this company on this -leased plant-not owned-were as follows:

That represents the earnings of this company. Now, we have the operation and management expenses, including necessary provision for capital, and the statement is as follows:

1 do not know why they should be allowed depreciation, because they did not own the elevator, but we will grant that they paid it and we will -allow them $29,955. Deduct $234,590, representing the expenses, from the earnings * of $446,308 and you have $211,718 net earnings of the company for one year. This, with an- invested operating capital of $100,000, which was every sou marquee they had in it, brings an unquestioned result of 211 per cent. After deducting the loss made in the sale of grain belonging to other people, amounting to $24,059, you have earnings of 187 per cent.

When the hardworking farmer or the hardworking citizen, whoever he may be, who is trying in these times to get along on a decent, honest profit, sees that these enormous profits have been made, is it not enough to make his blood boil? I do -not think this House should tolerate the practices to which I have referred, certainly they should not be perpetuated by this Bill. Not only are these profits made, Mr. Chairman, but they are made out of the very essentials of life.
I gave the overages the other day in the case of the Empire an,d Thunder Bay elevator. This company earned, in the years 1912 to 1917 inclusive, the following amounts and the following percentages respectively on capital: 28.50, 33.88, 10.75; 37.82, 43.54. Are these earnings not unreasonable for the class of business which is involved? The Thunder Bay and Empire companies are associated.

The overages of the Western Terminal Elevator Company for the years mentioned were the following: $60,871, $59,813, $10,182, $56,234, $94,590. The percentages are very similar to those of the preceding case.
As to the overages of, the Port Arthur Elevator Company, listen to these figures, Mr. Chairman, for the years I have mentioned: $185,193, $51,153, $50,369, $112,716, $388,057. These are the'overages, without the screenings, which the Port Arthur Elevator Company secured illegally, wrongfully from a moral standpoint. I lay it on the minister that action should be taken against these elevators to have them return to the exchequer of this country every cent illegally taken in overages. The minister and the Government must take cognizance of this matter. I -tried to bring it to the attention of the House; in February, from time to time 'but -I was prevented from doing so, or asked to let it stand, until private members' days had passed. I am not to-day going into a very detailed analysis of the matter, ibut( -I am trying to demonstrate the salient point that .this $15,000,000 that I have spoken of, every cent of which will foe found in the figures that I am quoting, -should foe returned to the exchequer of this country. If it is possible to find the legitimate owners of the money, it should be paid to them; if not, it should be credited to the Consolidated Revenue Fund. This thing should not be allowed to pass without action. It involves a matter which is gripping at the heart of the nation and Parliament dare not perpetuate the grievance as is proposed in this legislation.

, Now we come to the Canadian Government elevator, which is probably the largest elevator at the head of the lakes. I do not blame the minister in this connection, because I am quite certain that his time has been so fully occupied that he has not had an opportunity to analyze this voluminous report; but being somewhat of an accountant I have taken the trouble to analyze it and I am going to give the minister the benefit of the figures. I ask hon. gentlemen if they are going to allow a suggestion of that kind to
impose itself upon their intelligence in the face of these figures? The point I make . in all my argument is that under the clause of the Bill which provides that one-half of one per cent of the surplus may be retained, under no consideration should pass this House. Not only should no overage be allowed, but the amount of return on screenings should be limited to what might reasonably cover any possible shortage.
I now return to what the member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) has suggested- that possibly I am not warranted in designating these things as illegal.

speechtext:
My hon. friends may smile, but he that laughs last, laughs best. To make a fair comparison between this particular company that my hon. friend has singled out and other companies, you must take the cost of a 2,000,000 bushed plant on which to base your percentage of profits, so as to be fair to all concerned.
I can go into a business in connection with [iMr. Crerar.]
grain, the commission business for instance, and I need not invest $500 in it. All I need do is to rent an office and secure a desk or two, and a typewriter, my investment being probably $100 or $150, and may carry on a business according to the rules of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, on a commission charge which is sanctioned by the grain commissioners. I might make thousands and thousands of dollars in one season doing a straight commission business under regular charges, although I might not have $100 invested.
^ou must take a little broader view to get a proper basis on which to make a fair comparison. I do not know what kind of an elevator this 2,000,000 bushel elevator referred to is, and I cannot say what it would cost, but the approximate cost of such an elevator to-day would be in the neighbourhood of $900,000., This is not mere talk; I went to the trouble, just in order to inform the Committee, so that it will have the whole matter before it, of telegraphing Mr. C. D. Howe. This gentleman was the chief engineer of the Board of Grain Commissioners during the entire time of the construction of their elevators. He has been chief engineer for us and several other elevator companies at the head of the Lakes, and his figure is approximately $900,000. Let us take the auditors' figure of $100,000 which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has given us, as being the amount of working capital required. He is satisfied that they did not use that amount, so that that shows he is willing to read a little more into it than the auditors put in, to throw in a little on his own account, and that is indicative of something more. Let us take his figure of $211,000, and add the $68,000 they paid for rent for that building, and that gives us an amount approximately- not taking into account odd dollars and cents-of $279,000. Without taking into account the loss they made, but taking the entire amount, $279,000, and divide it into the capital expenditure of $1,000,000, and what do you find? You find in the neighbourhood of 27 or 28 per cent. Now, the Committee will notice that figures given by the hon. gentleman in connection with the other companies were based on the cost or value of the building-and these companies own the plants regarding which he gave the figures-and not on any rent they might pay. To make a fair comparison, you have to take the probable cost of the building, and this shows that while some of the other companies made 50 odd per

cent, in the case of the Grain Growers' Grain Company the percentage would be between 27 and 28 per cent. I think that is only a fair comparison to make. If they had owned this plant themselves, that would have been the actual condition, but they do not own it. Consequently, they have paid in the neighbourhood of 6 per cent on the cost of the building, and the balance is all charged up against the $100.000 of working capital. My hon. friend turned very indignantly on me when I simply asked him what I considered was a fair question, because this Committee cannot judge unless it knows the facts. Until one year ago, or it may be two-time goes so fast-when we had the annual meeting in Winnipeg with the Board of Grain Commissioners for the fixing of charges, percentage of screening to be retained by the elevators, and so on, we got them to reduce the amount of screenings that could be retained before a return had to be made to the farmer from 5 to 3 per cent. If this gentleman's returns had been made before the charge was reduced to 3 per cent, there could be absolutely no complaint.
If they were made after it was reduced to 3 per cent there would be cause for complaint, that is, if the figures given verbally to my hon. friend are correct; but unless this House knows whether it was before or after that the change was made from 5 to 3 per cent, we are not in a position to judge. That was the information I wanted. I was not trying to corner my hon. friend. We would have given almost anything to have had the hon. gentleman use exactly the same argument twelve or thirteen years ago that he has used on the floor of this House to-day. We tried our best then to get redress but it was not forthcoming. It is exactly what we farmers have maintained for years and years, in the old Parliament Building and in the city of Winnipeg. Hon. gentlemen may smile, but I would ask them to look up the records of the Canada Grain Commission to see what we have been asking for; I think those records contain almost verbatim reports. So this is nothing new, only that it was in a more intensified form twelve or fifteen years ago. The company with which the hon. member for Marquette is associated has asked for these reductions to be made. That company belongs, fike the other organizations, to the Canadian Council of Agriculture, which is the organ they speak through. We have asked the Grain Commission to make a change in these charges. We asked for the confiscation of the overages years and years ago. We knew what was being done; it is not a
new thing. Just so long as the present regulations exist my hon. friend will be able to make the same argument with regard to all the other companies that he has made in regard to this particular company.
I expect that at the end of this year the company of which I have the honour to be the president will have something similar to show. I do not know yet, but if they have not got it the only conclusion I can come to is that they have not been attending to their business. They will not have been dealing fairly with the shareholders and the customers if they have not got it. You can smile if you wish, but that is an honest statement, absolutely. It is simply working according to the regulations, and nothing else. We have exactly the same regulations in the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, where you have to make a certain fixed charge. The Board of Grain Commissioners can tell you that we have tried to have the present basis of a cent per bushel changed to a dollar basis, that is, a percentage basis, so that the unfortunate man who might have to sell his wheat at a certain time of the year when he could only get 60 cents or 70 cents a bushel would not have to pay as large a proportion as the man v ho sells his wheat for $1 a bushel. But we cannot get the change made; it is the same story all down the line. These people were handling grain on commission. We k iow it. We have also made money out of it, but it has come from our own people and gone back to them. As the hon. member for Marquette says, it is not an earning but a saving, which if these companies had not been in existence would have gone to other companies and so would have been lost to the farmers. I am not attempting to refute the hon. gentleman's argument at all. We know this has been going on, and it will continue to go on until the regulations are changed.

If we had not considered it a bad practice, we would not have attempted to get it remedied. The managers of the company my hon. friend has referred to have been fighting for just the same thing we have been fighting for, but if the regulations are not changed the same conditions will continue to exist. These people are not stealing; not at all; they are just taking everything that the regulations permit them to take out of the business. The regulations allow them to take those screenings and they take them. Would you have

' those screenings go to the United States, which buys a large amount of our screenings and have a lot of good wheat go with it for them to take out. The company would not be conducting their business properly if they allowed that. I suppose the hon. gentleman would think it an awful thing to make $300,000 or $400,000 on grain on a commission of one cent a bushel, but that is what the companies are doing; that is what the regulations allow them to do. We have consistently asked for the commission to be reduced, and it has been reduced to a certain extent, but it needs reducing a whole lot more. We also used to pay a cent a bushel for oats, but we have got that charge practically cut in two. The charge for barley has also been cut down.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The figures given by my hon. friend from Vancouver refer to dockages at the terminal elevators. Suppose a farmer ships his grain from an internal elevator. Is there a dockage there and also when the grain comes to the terminal elevator?

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
That will require going into the regulations just a little further. When the farmer brings his grain to the initial elevator his grain is docked if he sells it to the elevator. It is tested exactly the same as at the terminal elevator; the farmer is present and sees the grain tested. If he special-bins his grain and ships it himself the elevator is allowed, if I mistake not, on-e-half of one per cent for invisible shrinkage; that is what the regulations allow as a protection against loss in transit, and that is the only dockage made against the farmer. So the idea that he is docked at both ends is a mistaken one, except to the extent I have mentioned.
The hon. member said that overages were increasing. Of course, they are. The greater the volume of business, the greater the amount of overages. My hon. friend was not fair to the hon. member for Marquette when he said that that hon. gentleman had said they had to have this one-half of one per cent. He did not say any such thing. He is not asking for that. We have recommended that the charge be cut in two. You can take it all if you like. We 4 p.m. are not kicking; all we want is that every last cent shall go back to the farmer, and the sooner my hon. friend can assist us in bringing that about, the better we shall be pleased with him.
My hon. friend said that the figures of the Ogilvie people were much less. There is a good reason for that, and you will find 
it in the evidence that was given by tne manager of that company before the High Cost of Living Committee. He told where a certain amount of their screenings goes, which accounts for that company not having so much left. My hon. friend ' made another statement that I think is unfair to some of the companies.
I do not know what the practice is with the other companies, and I do not pretend to speak for them. I can, however, speak for our own company, in regard to the last year and during the time that we have been in business. In every case where there is an excess of 3 per cent, a return is made to the farmer. It is just possible, if you thoroughly investigate the return of the screenings, given by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, you will find that a large amount may have been returned to the farmer, that is, he may have been given credit for it. The hon. gentleman shakes his head, but I know that this happens.

Not at these figures I
quoted. These figures were the net, absolute, final return year by year to the elevators, after all rebates and reductions had been made.

I am not doubting for
a moment the sincerity and truthfulness of the hon. gentleman's statement, but it is just possible that those returns for screenings are not made out in a warehouse receipt at all. An elevator would get probably a thousand of those certificates. One certificate might call for a hundred pounds of screenings and another for five hundred pounds, while others might be for three or four hundred pounds, probably at different prices. The dealer would buy a number of these certificates and the terminal elevator company would then have an endless amount of trouble in making out these returns, while the cost in connection with it in most cases would probably be more than the screenings were worth. We considered this question with the Board of Grain Commissioners and that was the argument advanced by the terminal companies. There

is no certificate given for these screenings. It is just possible that that accounts for a lot of money received for these screenings that the elevator company has already given the farmer credit for.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Before this debate proceeds further it is due to the House and the country that the minister, who is primarily responsible for the administration of the elevators, should make a statement in answer to the charges of the hon. member for Vancouver. The terminal elevators are operated under the Grain Act assented to on 1st April, 1912, and are controlled largely by the Board of Grain Commissioners, who consist of three members appointed for a period of ten years. The country was told that these commissioners would be experts thoroughly informed on the trade. We find that the commissioners appointed were: Mr. Staples, who was formerly a member of this House from the province of Manitoba, and a supporter of the government of that day; Mr. Boyd, a lawyer of Montreal, who had been president of the Conservative Association in that city, and who I think had been twice candidate for the Conservative party, and Mr. Jones, I think, a practical man.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That is the present board. On the original board was Dr. McGill.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Dr. McGill had been on the board and had resigned to become secretary of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. -It is well to see how these men were appointed. It was provided that every officer employed under the authority of the board should be appointed by the minister on the recommendation of the board. The weighmasters, who have much to do with this work, are appointed by the minister, upon the recommendation of the board. These appointments are therefore made by the minister upon the recommendation of the board to him, so that obviously the Government are primarily and substantially responsible for the administration of these elevators; and if the charges made to-day by the hon. member for Vancouver are correct, we have never had in this House a more complete attack upon the Government by an hon. member who has loyally supported the Government of the day ever since he became a member of the House. In view of these considerations, therefore, I submit to the minister and to the committee that before the debate proceeds any further we are entitled to a statement from the minister concerning the administration of these elevators.

speechtext:
Regarding this matter, having lived for twenty or thirty years at the locus in quo, I may be able to contribute something to the debate. In the early days very little wheat came down and the rates were higher than now. The trouble in this whole matter is not that any one company has made overages. As the hon. member for Maple Creek says, they cannot do otherwise. The Government elevator is making overages and in that respect I do not think it would be quite reasonable to attack the member for Marquette because he is president of or holds some office in a company that has made money. They have all made money. Let us see how they made the money. The principle, as I understand it, is this-those more conversant with me business will correct me if I am wrong: In the first place, three-quarters of a cent is allowed for handling the grain in and outr of the elevators. In addition to that the grain in some cases has to be cleaned. In order to grade the grain for market purposes and to ascertain how much cleaning is necessary there is the inspection, and then arises what is called the dockage. Sometimes that dockage is 1 per cent, sometimes 2 per cent, and sometimes 5 per cent, or more. Dockage up to 5 per cent used to be allowed to the elevator for cleaning, and all over and above that had to be accounted for to the farmer. In the early days that was not so bad, because the volume of

wheat coming down was not so great. I remember well when the first bushel of wheat came down to Port Arthur. There was no elevator. We loaded into a warehouse in sacks and thence to the steamer in sacks. Then it began to increase to one jnillion, then to seven and nine millions, twenty, fifty, and a hundred millions, and so on. As this volume increased the dockage was reduced, it appears, from 5 to 3 per cent.

speechtext: What year?

speechtext: I cannot answer that question. Some one more versed in the matter will be able to say. I have been advocating on behalf of my district, its entire abolition. Because I believe it will be for the welfare of the elevator and for the welfare of the farmer to do so. The direct result would be if we abolish altogether this question of overages, that the producer will have private independent elevators at the head of the Lakes competing one against the other to buy his wheat, instead of waiting till it gets further East. There are two classes of elevators at the head of the Lakes; there is the terminal elevator and the private elevator. The terminal elevators are making money in this way because they are not allowed to speculate in wheat, but they get this surplus of wheat on their hands at the end of the year. How do they get it? The first reason, as has been mentioned, is the invisible shortage, which I think is something like thirty bushels to the car.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Thirty pounds.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I accept the hon. gentleman's correction of the slip, thirty pounds to the car. That goes to the elevator. The Committee can readily see that when there is a large volume of wheat coming down if you multiply the cars by thousands there is going to be quite a surplus on hand from that invisible shortage. In that case the elevator operators are allowed to do just as the miller did in the olden days who got his toll for grinding wheat; it is the same thing exactly. But now is the time to straighten the matter out, and it is not quite reasonable to be throwing around insinuations that anything improper has been going on; that is what I do not like about this thing. It is the regulations that makes such a thing possible, and now is the time to rectify it .
In addition to the invisible shrinkage there is the dockage. My wheat comes down and it is inspected. The man looks at it and docks me three per cent for dockage.

Dockage has no reference to anything in regard to a ship, but that percentage is docked by reason of dirty wheat or because of some wheat being of inferior quality. Now up to that point the elevator company takes that wheat, brings it into the house, cleans it and makes the best use of it, gives ninety-seven per cent back, and retains out of it three per cent damaged wheat or other matter which is what the screenings will amount to. After cleaning these screenings there will doubtless be some good wheat which may be added to the good wheat, if the elevator chooses, instead of selling it as screenings. It is this system which results in these terminal elevators necessarily having these overages at the end of the year and which is contrary to the principle of the Grain Act, because they are not supposed to be speculating in wheat, and they must sell it or get rid of it. Therefore, they have a self interest in this matter to a certain extent which ought to be disassociated from the warehousings business. As the hon. member from Maple Creek (Mr. Maharg) pointed out, the farmers have been steadily wanting to bring about a change in these methods and that is the reason, as I understand it, they went into the elevator business themselves. They are making money out of it, they cannot help doing so, but we should change the overage system. If three-quarters of a cent is too low for elevator charges, it would be better to increase it. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) says: " Protect us against wheat going off, or anything of tnat kind, in case we have a loss." It is hardly reasonable to ask that. The common carrier is not protected. He makes his contract and he gets "so much per" as the saying is for carrying out that contract, freight, or whatever it is, and he has to deliver the goods in the same condition in which he receives them. Why not have the terminal elevator in the same position as the common carrier. If three-quarters of a cent is not sufficient remuneration, let it be increased. Originally, it was not deemed advisable to make an increase. When there was but a small quantity of wheat coming down, a charge of three, four, or five cents a bushel for handling would seem large, but a higher dockage given for cleaning would not seem large, because there was a smaller volume coming to the elevator. Now that there is a large volume coming the price can be reduced subject to what I suggest, abolishing the principle of overages. The elevator operator should not have that wheat which does not belong to him, at the end of the year. If the price

of three-quarters of a cent is not sufficient to fairly protect him, why not increase it. They can get along then. The minister is moving along the right line, but I do not think he has gone far enough. I would like to see him sweep the whole principle out and have no overages whatever.

speechtext:
Before the minister replies, I would like to say a word or two if I may. It seems to me that the speech of my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Steven^) displays those qualities which I, as an old colleague of his, have long admired, of energy and courage, but is calculated, nevertheless, to arouse feelings and fears In the public mind which an understanding of the case would scarcely justify. I say that subject to correction because I am not at all sure that I understand the question myself. But I am going to take the liberty of putting the situation to the committee as it appears to me, after listening to every word that has been uttered to-day.
I want in the first place to clear up this thing as far as I can as regards the Grain Growers' Grain Company. That company, as I understand it, is simply a co-operative company by which the grain growers employ members of their own body in order to get the profits, whatever they are, for themselves. Well, the principle of co-operation has nothing wrong in it and, as far as profits from overages or anything else is concerned, so long as they go back to the farmers I do not think there will be any kick on their part. One of the misfortunes that might easily arise from the citation of figures running into the millions would be the use, in connection with those figures, of the very strong language which my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) has employed. One of the misfortunes that might easily arise, and that I am not at all sure is not meant to be caused to arise, is the impression that individual grain growers are becoming millionaires in the West. Now, in the Grain Growers' Company there are 35,000 shareholders. We were told by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar), in reply to a very pertinent question from the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), that that company with 35,000 shareholders has a paid-up capital of two millions and a reserve of a million and a half. If one divides the figures 35,000 into $3,500,000, then each of those grain growers would be a capitalist at the present moment, in reserve or in paid-up capital, to the magnificent extent of rather over $100. I think neither the Committee nor the country would
think that the grain growers are vastly criminal in being in possession of that sum of money each in paid-up capital and reserve in these times of profiteering. If I am wrong I shall be glad to be corrected, but that is the way the figures work out, so far as I have been able to work them out. If I am right, then I think I am safe in making the assertion that the grain growers are not becoming millionaries so far as the proceeds' of the operation of this elevator is concerned. What they are doing with the grain is exactly the same as any other grain grower is doing who hands his grain to a private company or to a private individual. The case would be more serious, much more serious, in the case of farmers, or grain growers who were selling their grain to private companies, because in that event whatever is made through these overages is going into the pockets of private individuals, and there some question of profiteering might arise. But I contend that no such question arises in connection with the company to which my friend from Marquette belongs, and nothing which has transpired here to-day reflects in the *slightest degree upon the character of my hon. friend or any of those who are associated with him.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Now I want to go a little more closely into this matter and see what there really is in the charges which have been brought, and, I may say, enforced upon the attention of the Committee by the use of very strong language. I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Stevens) said that $8,000,000 have been taken as the result of overages in a period of five years. I did not take notes but I think that was my hon. friend's assertion. Now it appears from the statement of the hon. member from Marquette (Mr. Crerar), and 1 think there is no doubt it is in accordance with the facts, that in the elevators where those $8,000,000 have accumulated, through overages being the system, good or bad, m those elevators, the charge for handling the grain is three-quarters of a cent a bushel. At the United States point of Duluth, where a large amount of grain is handled, the charge for handling that grain is li cents a bushel. I am told, incidentally, that they take overages there as well. So that, it would appear that the grain grovrers who are operating at these elevators are not getting on so badly at that, when compared with the grain growers of the United States who sell their grain at Duluth.

But, I want to give another view upon this question. In the five-year period during which it is alleged 8,000,000 bushels of grain have been accumulated through this terrible system of overages, probably a billion and a half bushels of grain were handled in the elevators concerned. If the difference between f cents a bushel and li cents a bushel be multiplied by a billion and a half it will be found that the charge for handling alone would have resulted in a perfectly proper legal payment, according to the charge at Duluth, of a profit of not 18,000,000 as the hon. gentleman alleges, but of $12,000,000 representing the extra three-quarters of a cent per bushel charged at Duluth. I think I am right in that statement; I think every figure ,1 have given in reaching my conclusion is absolutely correct. If the people at Duluth, on the same amount of grain, are paying for the actual handling of the grain $12,000,000, where only $8,000,000 is being made in overages on a smaller charge, then I must say that it would not appear that there is any good ground, in the general view of this question that I have endeavoured to take, for the extraordinarily strong charges which have been brought against the people operating these elevators, and who have been receiving what my hon. friend frofn Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) seems to consider the legitimate profits of a properly conducted trade.
I do not know that I need to say anything more. Indeed, I do not know that I can because I think the whole case is summed up in those salient figures and facts. But, I do want to say this: That if the short statement I have made is correct, although my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) worked himself into a state of indignation which the case did not call for, I very much question if the words " robbery," " illegality " and other strong language of that kind really applied. Let me say this: My hon. friend and I are old friends and he knows I am the last man to apologize, any more than he would be, for robbery or illegality. If there be a public grievance, if there be a public wrong, and my hon. friend points it-out to me, as long as we have seats in this House I will join with him in doing whatever I can to assist in the removal of that grievance. But I do not see, putting the case as I have just put it, that these strong terms of his need be applied.
One point I want to make, and it has already been made by the hon. member for Chateauguay and Huntingdon (Mr. Robb). If there has been robbery, if there has been

illegality, it has been carried out by, and according to the regulations, of tire Grain Commissioners, who are the appointees of the 'Government of this country. Certainly the indictment, judged by the strength of the language used in preferring it, w.as a tremendous indictment, because, in effect, it was a straight charge of illegal practices and robbery carried out under the auspices of the Grain Commission. We have all had a great deal to say against commissions, but I do not think there has ever been anything quite so strong said with reference to any individual commission as that which the hon. member for Vancouver has said against tnis particular commission. He, perhaps, did not mean it or see what he was doing until I asked him about it. The way in which he has done his duty is heroic in the extreme, and I admired his independence. I will be looking for him one of these days on the cross benches. I want to make it perfectly clear, if illegality and robbery have ' taken place under the auspices of this commission it is really a charge against the Government of the day. I leave the point at that; I do not urge it myself for a moment. As I have examined the case, I think the language is too. strong and therefore that the chEfrge is too strong, but I would repeat that if the charges lie at anybody's door they lie at the door of the Grain Commission, and I would join with my hon. friend from Vancouver in asking the Government either to explain the matter, or alter their legislation and clean up doings of this nefarious kind.
Mr. STEVEN'S: My hon. friend attempts to justify the charges made. I ask him: Does he consider that spread over a period of five years, the terminal elevators, performing a quasi public service, are earning too much when they get from 35 to. as high as 60 per cent and in one case 75 per cent?

Percentages are usually
deceptive. I have not the figures to show whether the percentages are as stated or not. I have given such figures as it has been within my power to give but without an analysis of the figures I am not in a position to answer my hon. friend's question. I am concerned with cleaning up a public grievance, doing all I can to put it right in the minds of the Grain Growers' Company and the private companies, and putting it right in the public mind as leading to the possibility of misconception that the grain growers, forsooth of all men, are making millions in these times of war and post war difficulties.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
there is no gainsaying the fact that the public are in a rather nervous and critical frame of mind at the present time, and I can hardly think that the discussion here this afternoop is going to remove many of the thoughts and suspicions that exist in their minds. I could not help but feel during the debate that has taken place, although I was not m the House when the original resolution came up, that there has been a great effort made to convey to the House that the transactions that were taking place should not be designated by such terms as stealing, robbery and illegal because they were done under the cloak of legislation passed Parliament and that the statutes of this country evidently permit things to be done the commission of which in private life would be considered as illegitimate, as illegal and liable to bring the parties who were practising them within the reach of the common law. It appears to me that it is up to this Government to see that remedies are provided and that they are provided immediately. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the statements which have been made in regard to overages. I have before me a paper published in Western Canada which gives the overages for the year 1917. According to this statement, the overages in fourteen elevators were as follows:

Wheat	 848,9'50
Oats	syoisot
Barley	 27,000
Flax		7S7
Mixed grains	 3,690,027
This aggregates an enormous sum which, according to the consensus of opinion, does not go back to those who should get the benefit of these overages.
The United Grain Growers' Ltd. has been mentioned	frequently this	afternoon.	1want it to be distinctly understood that I am not here	to	condemn	that	company.
It was absolute necessity that caused the farmers of the West to form that organization. The farmers were being deprived of their rights; they were being held up; they were suffering great injustice at the hands of dealers in grain in Western Canada. But the explanations that have been given this afternoon by some hon. members who are or have been connected with that company will hardly satisfy the public. The United Grain Growers Ltd. are to-day out to make profits the same as any other incorporated company. You may say that 35,000 farmers of Western Canada are members of that company, and that the profits
go back to them. That is all very true. But I have known other companies to be incorporated under similar circumstances; and you often find that the outsider who sometimes furnishes the largest Amount ol grain on products to the company does not receive the proportionate benefit that a smaller producer or non-producer receives because of his being a member of the company. However, I am not going into that question in detail. I want to point oul that these overages are unjustifiable, particularly in view of the fact that we have Government elevators in this country. In 1912, when the revision of the Grain Act was before Parliament, I took strong objection to certain features of the Act and particularly to the provision with regard to the screenings, which are a source of enormous revenues to the elevator companies. I brought the matter up in 1912, 1913, 1914, 1915, and 1917, but no effort has been made to remedy the difficulty. My contention then was and is to-day that hundreds of millions of dollars have been lost to this country as a result of the effort to realize a small temporary profit on the sale of the screenings, resulting in their distribution wholesale throughout the country. All along the railway lines of Canada, from one end of the country to the other, you will find masses of noxious weeds growing along the rights of way, caused by the dropping of seeds out of the cars which transport uncleaned grain over these lines. Scarcely a farm can be found in the old provinces or in the new that has not been poisoned because of the distribution of weed seeds by this and other means. Only two days ago we had representatives of some of the large milling corporations before a committee of this House. According to the sworn evidence which was there given, it has been for years the customs of these milling companies, some of which have a string of elevators all over Western Canada, to take the screenings of these elevators and mills and run them in with the bran and shorts and other mill feeds. Before wheat can be milled for the manufacture of flour, every atom of weed seed must be taken from the wheat; it is absolutely necessary that the wheat shall be as clean as possible. The custom has been to run these screenings through duplex grinders which are supposed to grind the stuff down fine, and the millers are then permitted, by Act of Parliament, to run this stuff back into the bran and shorts provided that not more than 2,500 vital noxious weed seeds are left in each 100 pounds of bran and shorts. You would think that gives them

enough latitude. But they can in addition grind as much of these screenings as they see fit, provided they destroy the vitality of the weed seeds and provided they have sufficient protein, fat and fibre in their bran and shorts to comply with the Feed-stuffs Act. The statement was made the other day by the head of one of these big milling firms'that the quality of their bran and shorts had been improved as a result of mixing these ground screenings in with them. We all know how impoverished and how thin the bran is that we get from the milling companies to-day. Pure bran is perhaps the most valuable feed that is used in connection with the production oi dairy products; it is fed more largely by the dairy men than any other food except hay and ensilage; and it is only fair to those engaged in dairy farming that they should get this product in a [DOT] pure state, not in an adulterated state, as is permitted under the present law. But although the millers are permitted to have 2,500 of these weed seeds in a sack of bran or shorts, they go much further than that. I happened to pick up the report of the Inland Revenue Department for July, 1918, the day the millers' representatives were here, and 1 found that two of the men who were present on the occasion of the examination of the millers before the committee were representatives of two of the big firms mentioned in this report. This report of the Dominion analyst shows that on no less than eight occasions during the month covered by the report, these two big companies had exceeded the limit which I have mentioned. I am not going to go into the matter in detail; I will just mention one case, that of the Ogilvie Flour Mills Company, in ordei to show the extent to which this adulteration takes place. In this case, 864 lamb's quarters, and 96 tumbling mustard seeds to the pound were found in excess of the amount permitted. The report of another inspector shows that 1,392 lamb's quarters, and 768 tumbling mustard seeds to the pound were found in excess of the amount exempted. The remarkable thing is that this has been going on for years, and although reports setting forth these facts have been filed in the department from year to year, these men say that in not one instance have they been prosecuted for violation oi the law. They have become so bold that they now openly admit that they are running these screenings in and that they do not think there is any danger in doing so. But several departments, under this Administration, as well as under previous Governments, have been aware of the 
fact that live stock in very large numbers have been poisoned and have died as a result of being fed with this adulterated stuff that is being sold to the farmers. The people of Canada are advised to practise rigid economy. I reiterate what I have stated on several occasions with regard to this, namely, that hundreds of millions of dollars are being lost to the people of this country as a result of the carelessness we have shown in this regard. Screenings are something that must be taken care of by the Government through the Grain Commission at those elevators, and they must be cleaned and recleaned to the extent that there will not be any danger of feeding the stuff to livestock nor any danger of having the farms of this country contaminated by the foul weed seeds that have for years been distributed in this way. But some hon. members will say: What will these big milling companies lose as a result of this? See what the farmers of Western Canada will lose as a result of it. We had an admission from the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) to-day that in some instances as much as 20 per cent of the grain shipped out to elevators consists of weed seeds. If that be the case, there is no reason why screens cannot be put into the separators which thresh this grain so that the great bulk of these weed seeds may be taken out. I know threshers in the West and elsewhere, who are paid by the bushel, would not like to do that, and they will permit the screens to get clogged. But it is absolute carelessness on the part of the farmers of Western Canada to permit that condition to continue; they are paying freight rates on this dirt being shipped to the elevators, and in the end this will react against them. It is not in our interest nor in the interest of the public generally that this should be permitted. The screenings of the elevators should be screened to the finest possible degree so as to eliminate all these weed seeds. I find to my amazement that even during, the past year, notwithstanding the fact that we had so experienced an agriculturist as the hon. member for Marquette at the head of the Department of Agriculture, this thing has been allowed to continue, and that instead of stamping it out, it has been encouraged to the extent that the Government have been purchasing thousands of tons of these screenings and selling them to the farmers of this country through the Department of Agriculture. They have not taken the precaution to see that that stuff was ground

at the elevators, where there is ample provision for grinding it, but it is being dis- * tributed throughout Ontario and the other provinces to whoever may be so foolish as to buy it. You can understand people engaged in poultry or sheep raising or something of that kfnd, when feed is so high, buying this stuff and feeding it, and as a result, many of these noxious weeds are spread throughout the country. I find that up to December 1 of last year alone 8,094 tons of this stuff had been purchased, and to my amazement I find that wild oats constitute nearly 11 per cent of this unground stuff that is being shipped throughout Canada and that the Government have entered into a contract to purchase from the Elevator Company at $35 a ton. I believe the allowance made for screenings to the farmers for the excess over 3 per cent is $15 per ton. Yet it is turned over to the Government at $35 per ton. I realize that that seems rather remarkable, but this is for recleaned screenings, without the bulk of the fine black weed seeds which undoubtedly constitute a considerable part of it. But it is the part that should be eliminated and can easily be eliminated by the threshers on the farm and that should be destroyed by the farmers when threshing takes place; if not there then at the elevators and mills.
Let me quote from a bulletin issued by the Inland Revenue Department with regard to bran and shorts under date of January 20, 1919:
We have for months past been receiving numerous complaints with reference to the adulteration of bran and shorts, and have had samples of the same that certainly justify the complaints. The bran is adulterated by mixing with oat hulls and all sorts of rubbish. Shorts, in many cases, is simply bran, re-ground so as to make it fine.
And so forth. There is just another feature of this to which I want to refer very briefly. The Department of Agriculture had the present director of experimental farms investigate the matter several years ago. He went into it very thoroughly and presented a very interesting report. Referring to this matter, he states regarding the millers:
If he grinds his screenings fine enough to destroy the vitality of all the noxious weed seeds, the miller is within his legal lights in mixing this pulverized material with his byproducts, provided that such admixture does not alter their chemical composition to such an extent that they no longer comply with the requirements of the Feeding Stuffs Act	-
The Dominion and provincial Departments of Agriculture receive each year many complaints of the death or serious injury to the health of
animals which the owners of the stock attribute to the feeding of bran, shorts and chop-feed.
It is quite well known to all the stock men in this country that such is the case.
Jif go, many animals die as the result of the feeding of this stock. This being so one can understand how many animals which do not die have their vitality seriously impaired from eating it, and the product does not give the results which the purchaser expects it should. When I brought this matter up last in 1914, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) made this statement in reply to my argument on that occasion:
The Provincial Governments have their parts to do in the matter, and they are moving in that direction; the Department of Agriculture of the Dominion and the departments of agriculture of the several provinces co-operate in this work. Whatever can be done by the Grain Board, and-after they have mapped out their work in this matter-whatever can be done by Dominion legislation to diminish this pest, will he done. And I hope to he able, at the next session of Parliament, to give a fairly clear idea as to what we think can be done by the Grain Board and through Parliament in this direction.
I have been waiting patiently, expectantly, to see if something would be done, and I must say that when the present amendments to the Grain Act were brought down, without any provision being made for taking care of this stuff at the elevator, I was disappointed. I can only say that I believe the minister has not fulfilled his duty in respect to the farmers and grain growers of this country in reference to this matter. What would you think of the medical authorities of a country pretending to be attempting to stamp out disease by providing isolation hospitals, putting those afflicted with a disease in them, and at the same time collecting the germs of the disease and mailing them out over the country? You concentrate this stuff at the elevators when you reclean the grain, and there is no reason why it should not be destroyed at that point, after you reclean it to such an extent that no injustice will be done to the party who has supplied the grain. This is a matter that I know has not received much attention by Parliament, and it is one that will be passed over lightly by many hon. members. It is a question in which some of the great corporations of this country are vitally interested, and it is also one that affects every individual farmer in this country, because in the days to come, you may rest assured that agriculture will have to be carried on on a scientific basis in Canada. The hope for the future rests pri-



marily on Canada's vast agricultural domain.
Live stock raising is the only hope for our farmers. You may exploit the soil to your heart's content, but the day will come when you will have to replenish the fertility which you have taken out of it, and this can only be done by entering upon a system of farming of which live stock will be the main feature. You may not call it stealing or robbery or illegal to pass out this poisonous stuff to our farmers, but I think if we had Webster here to-day he would have to change his definition of stealing. He would not say that it
5 p.m. -was taking something from some one without his consent; but, by Act of Parliament; that might be his definition. I am sorry to have to say these things. I have waited patiently for years to see some reform made. If one-half of what the hon, member for Vancouver has said is true, with regard to overages, I do not see how action can be delayed any longer. It is a remarkable thing that I have not been able to get a copy of the audit that was made of the elevator companies for these years referred to, although I have endeavoured to do so, and knew that such an audit existed.
I contend that this is too important and vital a question to be passed over lightly oven in the last days of this session. Even if it means our remaining here a little longer than was anticipated, I think the mill feed regulations should be changed, and we should prohibit the adulteration of bran and shorts by the millers. There is no justification for permitting him to adulterate as at present permitted by the regulations. He should also be prosecuted where he has so often violated the present law. It cannot be adulterated without his knowledge and consent. Consequently, there is no justification for it. The big millers the other day expressed their astonishment that they were violating the law in this regard. They also expressed the view that it would be justifiable, and in fact the part of wisdom for the Government, if what I expressed was true, and I showed conclusively by Government reports that it was true, to prohibit the running of that stuff back into their bran and shorts. I heard of several cases this past winter where stock have died as a result of eating this poisonous stuff. Let me quote two cases from the Agricultural Gazette published by this Government. They are from a report made by the Director of Experimental Farms when the hon. member for Marquette was Minister of Agriculture:
[Mr. Sutherland.!
A case has recently been brought to our notice which corroborates this (the poisoning of stock). A sample of shorts was sent in for analysis, the farmer complaining that as a result of feeding it, two of his pigs had died. Large quantities of finely ground mustard seeds were found in the sample. A reply to our request for a statement of symptoms ran as follows:
