A sample of shorts was received at the laboratory from a farmer. He and his neighbour had bought some from the same lot and each had given one feed to their pigs. The meal was eaten, and in a few hours all the pigs-eight belonging to one man and ten to the other-were dead.	An analysis1 of the
sample showed 1.7 per cent by weight of whole Wormseed Mustard seeds in addition to those which had been ground.
I will not weary the House by citing further cases, but would simply say that the record's of the various branches of the Government are loaded up with information which goes to show that they have absolute knowledge of the correctness of the statements, which I have made here this afternoon, and I must say that it does not reflect very much credit upon the Government that steps- have not been taken to provide redress long before this.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The statement just made by the hon. member (Mr. Sutherland) is an extremely interesting one, and I am not disposed to find any fault with it whatever. In fact, I think this is a subject which should have had the consideration of the -Government long before this. Of course, if it were not for the great quantities of noxious weeds which a-ppear on Canadian farm lands, the question of dockage, and, therefore, the question of overage, would not arise. My attention, however, had never been drawn to this matter, and it never entered my mind that it should be dealt with this session in the amendments to be made to the Grain Act. It may be that this is a matter that comes under the Department of Agriculture, which has jurisdiction over the subject of noxious weeds. I can only promise my hon. friend who has just taken his seat that I shall direct the attention of the proper department to this, subject at the earliest opportunity, because I think it is clearly a case for immediate action and legislation.
Now just a word on the general subject we have been discussing this afternoon.
I think that altogether too much heat has been aroused. The matter of overages does not involve the question of illegality or robbery or dishonesty at all. It is not in contravention of the Grain Act that the elevators obtain these overages. My hon.

friend quoted from the Auditor's Report to the effect that the sale made by elevators of these overages constituted an offence under the Act. The report states that to be the opinion of the counsel of th* auditors, Price, Waterhouse & iCompany. Now il am not disposed to accept that opinion as being correct and, if it were a correct one, I would say: Amend the Act so as to make the sale legal, because it would be absurd to allow the elevators to earn these overages and then say that they shall not sell them, or that if they attempt to sell them it will be illegal. If it is illegal to dispose of these overages, it should be made legal, so long as overages are permitted.
My hon. friend (Mr. Robb) seemed very anxious that I should make a defence of the Government in this matter. I do not think the Government are obliged to make any defence in this matter. I do not think the Government can be properly or justly accused of maladministration of the Grain Act, nor do I think the grain commissioners are open to accusation. There is no country in the world which handles the grain business with a greater degree of efficiency than Canada. There is no country in the world which has such an elaborate and almost perfect system as ours for handling grain. There are overages, of course, and with the high prices that have prevailed for wheat during the last three or four years the overages have been higheT than usual, measured in dollars and cents; and when you have a big crop and the elevators are handling a vast quantity of wheat the overages are laTge. In 1915 there was a very small wheat crop and the elevators only made 1 per cent, clear of overages and screenings, upon the capital invested. Counting screenings, they made 4 per cent, but taking their elevator charges, screenings, and overages, they made only 8 per cent. Hon. gentlemen will realize that the immense overages which have occurred during the period of five years referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. Stevens) are not a permanent factor in the grain trade, because conditions during those five years will not remain constant.
After all, what does " overages " mean in actual practice? It means, as the hon. member for Port Arthur said, a system established by usage, by which the elevator man receives a part of his elevator charges in kind, just as in the days when I was a boy the millers kept in payment for their services a portion of the grain sent to their mills to be ground. That has obtained in this country for years and years
and everybody is aware of the practice.
It may be wrong, or right. I am disposed to feel, in regard to this, as in regard to other matters, that gradually we shall reach what will be a perfect solution of the whole problem, aifd very likely in the course ol two or three years we shall have a cash-tariff for elevators. Many representations-were made to the department this year on this particular issue, and in view of these and the report of this auditor, I felt bound to introduce .some legislation at the present session, although possibly it might well have remained over until next session. Indeed, I am quite willing now to drop the Bill if many hon. gentlemen think that this should be done. I had personal interviews with representatives of the Council of Agriculture, which body I think at least represents the grain growing farmers of the West. I was also interviewed by those representing the elevator interests, who informed me that they were quite willing to-abolish overages absolutely and establish a cash tariff. This they are willing to do to-day. Some of the representatives of the Grain Growers of the West, however, stated to me that they preferred that the elevator should, in part at least be paid for their services by overages. As has been pointed out, the elevator charge in Canada is J of a cent per bushel for the services that have been mentioned this afternoon-lower than anywhere else on the North American continent save the port of Baltimore, where it is a little lower. This charge of I of a cent needs to be increased or supplemented if the elevators do not receive some of the overages. I desire to deal with this matter in some way at this session, but I am not prepared to ask Parliament, in face of the representations made to me, to enact that overages should be absolutely abolished and a cash tariff established. I do not presume to say that the abolition of overages might' not be the proper thing to do, but I do not propose to do it at this session because I do not personally know enough	about	the question;
and at least until the Grain Growers in the West, who are more interested than any one else, make representations to the department to have overages absolutely abolished, I will not take such a step. At any rate, I would like further time to consider the matter. In this Bill is contained a clause (No. 2) which provides for a maximum of overages of | of 1 per cent. I intend to ask the committee to make it I of 1 per cent, which would reduce it somewhat. After, say, one season's experience, and after we have had

an opportunity to see how it works, we shall be in a better position to deal with the matter. I hope my suggestion will be received favourably by the committee because there are some portions of the Bill which it is desirable to enact. However, if there is very much opposition to it I would prefer letting it stand altogether. I am afraid that members of the committee fear that these overages are obtained by some subterranean and dishonest method. The hon. member for Huntingdon would apparently throw the blame on the Government or on the Grain Commission. Well, the Grain Commission has absolutely no more to do with the creation of overages than has the hon. gentleman.

speechtext: What I said was, that if the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver is correct, then the Government are primarily responsible, because all the employees who handle the grain are appointed by the Government.	_

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is quite true that they are appointed by the Government, and their work may be performed with absolute accuracy and efficiency, and still you might and would have overages. Now how do overages occur?

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: How does the minister come to reduce the one-half to three-eighths of one per cent?

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
In a purely arbitrary manner, and in a spirit of compromise. One-quarter has been suggested by some. Representatives of the farmers have said that it should not be reduced to the point where the elevator companies would ask the Grain Commissioners to increase their tariff rates. I do not consider myself competent just at the moment to determine the exact jpercentage to allow, and the percentage of three-eighths was just reached arbitrarily. How do overages arise? It is a very complicated matter, particularly for a layman, to attempt to make an explanation of. I shall read to the committee the report of the auditors upon this point which will make it clearer than I could possibly state it. Before I dio so, however, I may say that the grain is inspected as ,it arrives at Winnipeg.
A sample of wheat is taken from every car and is placed in the hands of our inspectors. The inspection at Winnipeg is a very severe one. A small quantity of wheat is taken from a car and is put through a very fine sieve, and the inspectors determine the proportion per bushel of deleterious matter in the wheat. That is done with scrupulous 
care by a special officer of the Grain Board and the process is carried out with accuracy. The inspector can measure yvith precision the amount of deleterious matter or defective wheat in the sample. He finds, say, on the average, one- per cent of dockage to be made by reason of foreign matter in the wheat. Later on all this wheat goes to the terminal elevators at the head of the Lakes. That wheat is all mixed up, and it goes, in large quantities, in chutes from the elevators directly on board the ship. It is impossible to inspect the wheat while going out of the terminal elevator, with the same degree of accuracy as the inspector at Winnipeg inspects the wheat, and in the main that is the reason for the overages. The auditors in their report set forth their views as to the cause of overages:
(1.) In cars of high grade grain which contain a small proportion of foreign matter, the inspector almost invariably places a dockage of 1 per cent.
The inspector gets that dockage of one per cent by inspecting a small sample, and which inspection he therefore can carry out with accuracy; but when wheat comes to the elevators at the rate of millions of bushels a day, -I imagine that cannot be done, and consequently the inspection there is not of so severe a character. The auditors say further:	-
(2.) The dockage is not stated in fractions. For instance, if the inspection showed a percentage of foreign matter of from 2% to 3% a dockage of 3% would he placed on the car.
Of course that would he another source from which the elevators would earn a dockage. Let us suppose that the actual dockage was 2J per cent. As a matter of fact the dockage would foe three per cent in the inspection report, whereas in actual practice the elevator, would not find that quantity of deleterious matter to clean from the wheat, and of course that would account, theoretically at least, for the difference between two and seven-eighths per cent and three per cent. The report goes on -to say:
(3.) While the percentage of dockage placed on the car, as the -wheat arrives at the elevator, is estimated to eliminate all foreign matter, it is a fact that the grain leaving the elevators contains a certain small proportion of dust, although the grain is " commercially clean." '
That is, the inspection at the terminal elevator is not so severe and thorough as the inspection at Winnipeg. The auditors go on to say:
(4.) It was noticed that the overages occurred chiefly in the higher grades of wheat. An explanation which has -been offered is that the cars on which the 1% dockage is placed

are mostly of high-grade grain on which the actual dockage -would be less than 1 per cent. It would also seem to be a fact that in an average season the crop is mostly high-grade grain.
(5.) It would appear that under the present tariff any efficiently managed elevator should show an overage. It might be possible for an elevator by not using sufficient care in recovering good grain from its screenings, to show a deficit of grain at the end of the season, but, in such a case, the revenue from screenings should be above normal by reason of a quantity of good grain being left therein, thus commanding a higher price.
Such are the reasons given by the auditors for the creation of these overages. I am not attempting to defend the system; it is an old one that has grown up and it may not be satisfactory to the grain-growing and the elevator interests; but in the past amendments have from time to time been made, and, as I have already stated, in my judgment the time will soon be reached when a cash tariff for elevator services should be put into effect. To that, as previously stated, the elevator people do not object; the only objection I have had to it came from the farming interests in the West, who prefer paying for a part of the elevator charges in this way. As a matter of fact this loss is largely borne by the grain dealers, because I would imagine that in 75 per cent of the cases the farmer sells his wheat to the country elevator, or some grain dealer, and the loss, if any, is not suffered by the farmers, but, in most cases, by the grain dealers.
Mr. ,A. K. MA'CfLEAN: Perhaps three-eighths of one per cent.

I suppose a great deal more might be said about this matter by me, but I feel there are a great many other gentlemen in the House who understand the subject much better than I do. However, I wish to protest against the suggestion that these overages occur through illegal or dishonest dealings. The Committee at least should not have that impression, and I would submit for its consideration that for the present at least we might make what is probably a step forward this session and fix three-eighths of one per cent as the proportion, instead of one-half of one per cent. Then at the next session of Parliament the matter could be further considered, particularly with the idea of ascertaining what would be the view of the grain producers of the West in the matter of establishing a cash tariff for elevator charges, and abolishing overages altogether.

speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion this afternoon, and I certainly appreciate very much the fact that we have had hon. members, representing other provinces than those in the West, springing up in this House in defence of the farmers' interests. For a number of years we have been making representations to Parliament asking that arrangements might be made whereby we would obtain something like an equitable method of handling our grain, and we have made progress. It has not been all discouragement that we have met with. Some times the battle has been severe and the progress not very marked, but nevertheless progress has been made-progress that has been of great advantage to the,farmers of the West. A number of statements have been made this afternoon, startling statements, from which it might appear that there were serious difficulties in the way and that great losses have been sustained by a certain class of people by reason ol those difficulties. But, Sir, when you institute an analysis and get down to the real facts in the case, those statements are not as serious as they appear to be on the surface. There is loss, we admit, and we have-felt it all along. For years we have been trying to overcome that loss and we have been moving towards a solution of it, and I am sure the impetus that has been given to the movement to-day will help us materially in getting a more satisfactory adjustment of matters in the future.
Let us look at the situation for a moment. Some years ago we had a warehouse commissioner, whose duty it was to supervise the operation of the warehouses through which this grain passed. We felt at the time that there was a great deal of looseness in connection with the warehousing of the grain, and that opportunities existed in connection with that warehousing for taking from the farmers a percentage of grain of which they should not be deprived. We are now moving towards a system of more definite supervision. Some years ago we secured the appointment of the grain commission with the idea that the work of supervision should be in the hands of men

who had no direct interest whatever in the grain or in the warehouses, and who would carefully watch the operations that took place in connection with those warehouses.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Personally, I have had a great deal of difficulty in reaching the conclusion that it was necessary to have an Appeal Board. However, the view in the West was very strongly in favour of the creation of such a board. The administration of the Grain Act costs the country nothing; in fact I think the treasury has a surplus this year on that account of about $80,000. If the creation of this board will cause the grain producing interests of the West to have greater confidence in the thoroughness of the inspection, I should not be disposed to find fault with the establishment of an Appeal Board. It should not be a very expensive body to carry along; although they must be properly paid, they need not receive very high salaries. At any rate, the grain interests, one way or another, will pay for it; the cost will not fall directly upon the Dominion treasury. men being appointed to different positions, but no matter what Government is in power, it is some Government favourite who is lobbying for the position and it is some Government favourite who gets it.

speechtext: Well, some of them may have an eye on the plum, though I am not saying they have. Under the present system the members of the Survey Board are appointed, onedialf by the Grain Exchange, the men who handle the grain and who have put their money into the business, and the other half by the Ministers of Agriculture of the provinces which are more particularly interested, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta. speechtext:
This request came, as the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. A. K. Maclean) has said, from the farmers. The farmers did not make the request without giving the matter careful consideration. They experienced some difficulties in connection with the operations of the Survey Board, and after full consideration of the matter they came to the conclusion that it was necessary to have an Appeal Board the members of which would be separated entirely from the men directly interested in the handling of the grain. The Survey Board was not so separated. While they were appointed as my hon. friend (Mr. Robb) states, the members were selected from men who were directly interested and employed in the grain business. It has been felt for years that the farmers have not had that confidence in the Survey Board which would encourage them to make an appeal to that board, even though they felt they were not getting justice. It has been their view that in appealing to this board they were appealing to men who were directly interested and whose decision might be more or less influenced by that interest. In view of this circumstance, and
[Mr. Robb.}
of the experience of Minneapolis in this regard, we felt that we were justified in asking the Government to appoint an Appeal Board which would be Independent of any grain interest and the business of which would be to give that work full and careful attention.
We believe there will be a large number of appeals, when confidence is inspired as to the ability of the Appeal Board to handle this work. As regards the qualifications of the men who shall sit on this board, there is not very much in the remark made by my hon. friend opposite (Mr. Robb), that the farmers may perhaps be looking for a plum on this point. The farmers realize that the man who is going to qualify for this position must be one who has gone up through the different grades, through the inspectorate. To be properly qualified for this work, he must start at the beginning of the business and go up step by step, so that he will have a thorough knowledge of grain, and very few farmers claim that they are in a position to qualify for an appoints ment of that kind. They were not looking to any personal interest when they made this request; they were looking to allay a state of dissatisfaction and unrest that has arisen in the country because they believed the parties on the Survey Board might have a direct interest in the grain they were surveying, and the feeling was that justice might not be done to the producer by that arrangement. Consequently, they had made this request for an Appeal Board. Furthermore, as has bee.n stated by the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. A. K. Maclean), there is no reason why this Committee should demur against the establishment of this board. It is no charge on the country; the farmers who are making the request for the board are the ones who are paying and who expect to pay for it.

speechtext: There are just two things in this section with which the Canadian Council of Agriculture do not quite agree. subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.

The suggestion ol the hon. gentleman had been before me prior to the discussion of this Bill. Personally I think the method here provided is preferable to that he suggests. The Minister of Trade and Commerce at present is responsible for the administration of the Grain Act, and that being so, I think he should be responsible for naming the members of the Appeal Board. As a matter of practice the department would, of course, request all interested bodies to suggest names of persons for appointment to the board, and I think the department would always be found willing to give careful consideration 'to any nominations that might be made by the Canadian Council of Agriculture, the Grain Exchanges, or any other interested parties. The department's only interest would be to see that the appointments made were satisfactory to all interested parties, because if they were not satisfactory, it would simply mean more or less worry and anxiety for the department.
I think, therefore, there should be no difficulty in the Governor in Council making appointments which will be satisfactory to every person concerned. It is a bad practice for outside persons to name the personnel of bodies created by a statute

which is being administered by the Dominion Government. I took this position when some representatives of the 'Council of Agriculture were before me some two or three months ago, and I think they were fairly well satisfied with my suggestion. I would prefer leaving the section as it is.

speechtext: I do not want to have to press our views too much, but I think that if we had had the recommending of the Board of Grain Commissioners it would be differently constituted. With regard to the location of the Appeal Board, this is of more vital importance to us than all the rest of the amendments put together. Failing to have the board located in Winnipeg, we should feel that the amendments were practically of no value to us, It may be possible that we place too much value on ' the Appeal Board, but it is our hope not only that it will achieve success in the matter of the actual inspection of grain, but that, working in conjunction with the laboratory carried on by the department, we shall be able to secure other information which so far has not been available-at least, that has- not been afforded us. We have been trying to get certain information and the laboratory has not been able to furnish it, at least it has not been made public. We would like to have the Appeal Board situated in Winnipeg in order that they may be right on the job where the grain is marketed, sampled and inspected. I cannot, therefore, see how the Appeal'Board will operate successfully in any place other than where the business is done. If the sample market is established in Winnipeg there will be no possibility of success in having the board anywhere else, as that is where the inspection will be carried on. subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I have additional matter to bring before the committee, arising out of amendments to the Grain Act. There has been a strong feeling growing up in the West against certain practices that have obtained in connection with the handling of our grain on the Winnipeg Grain Exchange. In order to correct these practices the Grain Growers last winter introduced legislation into the provincial house, thinking that was the proper place to apply to for a remedy. Upon the introduction of the Bill, however, it was found to be ultra vires, and they were assured that the matter should be dealt with in the Federal Parliament, it being interprovincial, or rather federal, in its character. The Canadian Council, having considered the matter fully, decided that it should be brought before this House in connection with the amendments to the Grain Act. Consequently, that is my reason for bringing the subject up at this time. It was thought at first that a Bill covering the whole question should be introduced, but upon reconsideration it was decided that the best way to proceed would be through amendments to the Grain Act. Under the circumstances, I wish to place before the committee a statement, following that up by a recommendation that we have to offer. In order to be as concise and brief as possible, I would like to present our view's on this question in manuscript form:
Speculation in Wheat.
For some years the protest against questionable kinds of speculation in wheat has been widespread and persistent. This protest had reached an acute stage hy the end of the year 1915, and producers of grain, through their various organizations, were making strenuous efforts to have this abuse controlled1. Conditions changed at that time, which change was brought about by the war, making it necessary to establish a fixed price for grain. With the fixed price there came also a regulation of charges to be paid to grain handlers in order that a reasonable living might be given to all parties directly Interested in the* handling of grain, while at the same time it precluded the possibility of speculation. In this way the pernicious practice which was. in vogue, and which was the cause of such serious complaint amongst producers, was eliminated, and because of these fixed prices the evil referred to has been obliterated. Now the war is over, and there is an agitation for a return to old conditions by the re-establishment of an open market, it is very desirable that such legislation be introduced, as will guard against the evils that had grown up to which I have already referred.
To quote from the views expressed by the Manitoba Grain Growers' Association at their convention, I give you the following:-

" Viewing with a large measure of concern the restoration of conditions which make possible speculation in the handling of our chief food products, this association desires to call the attention of the Government to the serious evil which has crept in along these lines, and to ask that provision be made in the Grain Act that will eliminate this improper speculation."
The United Farmers of Alberta express the same concern and desire to voice their protest against " scalpers and speculators taking toll which frequently amounts to more than the profits of the producer." They demand that legislation be .passed confining the dealing in all exchanges and elsewhere to cash grain and sales for actual future delivery of grain and grain products1; and that steps he taken to provide the necessary credit to finance all farmers who have grain for sale until such time as it is possible for them to market the same. To speak more specifically, this concern is not a matter of narrow prejudice against a usage which may be comparatively harmless. It is the protest of a large proportion of our people, including many who are thoroughly familiar with the conditions and who know the nature and the effects of the evil against which they protest. It is a protest against a spurious form of business which has been preying upon the legitimate grain business of the country and has come to constitute a serious blot upon the business and general life of our times.
What, then, are some of the things against which protest is made? Negatively, we do not protest against nor make an attack upon, the Grain Exchange. With the important and legitimate work carried on by the Grain Exchange there is a very strong desire to co-operate. It is the illegitimate and indefensible modes of dealing that in some cases are carried on in connection with the exchange that are aimed at. The exchange itself, for the protection of its legitimate operations, should be the strongest supporter of this1 contention; and many of the members of the Exchange are co-operating with us in the desire to overcome this difficulty. We are not attacking those legitimate and common forms of dealing in grain known as "hedging." It is recognized that hedging is a necesary and perfectly legitimate practice. Nothing therefore that may ibe said in support of my proposal has any reference to that practice. There is no intention or desire that it should in any way be interfered with. Let that fact he fully recognized.
The thing complained of is the speculative trading in futures in which there is no actual or potential exchange of values, which often does not in any sense or in any degree represent actual wheat; the paying of a sum to be treated rffe a " margin " and the adding to that sum as the market advances in order to hold the " deal," and the frequent manipulation of the market which is occasioned in connection with these operations.

speechtext: The association protests against this because it is stock jobbing?

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is not jobbing at all; it is speculation in margins. They put up a small sum of money and speculate in margins.

speechtext:
Do I understand the
Grain Exchange is in sympathy with the demand made by the farmers?

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The complaint is against certain associations who deal in grain in connection with the Grain Exchange?

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Certain practices which have grown upon the Grain Exchange.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Would the hon. gentleman give me a concrete case, as an example, so that I might better understand the
matter?

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Parties go upon the
market, simply put up a certain amount of money, so many cents a bushel, and deal in margin. If the grain goes up they put in more, while, if the grain goes down, they reverse the operation. They are simply speculating in margin, they have no grain, no intention of having grain but, by their manipulation of the market, we contend that they mislead the public in regard in grain values. The statement I was reading proceeds:
It has for years1-apart from the Period ol fixed prices-(been the common experience that when the wheat 'begins to come in in quantity early in the season there are those who find it to their advantage to use every effort to depress the market; and the " hammering " process *begins and is usually effective in running the price down, to the disadvantage of the producer. The chief burden of this depression is borne by the farmer who is hard up-the man who is starting or who has not yet secured stable financial standing and must dispose of his crop to meet current debts. The fact that he is compelled to take a price often ten cents a bushel lower than would otherwise foe paid is tremendously important to him. The well-established or wealthy farmer who can hold his grain for a later rise in price is not so seriously affected; but the man who has difficulty in keeping his head above water has his lot made very hard by this operation.
It may be argued that there usually is a lowering process which occurs naturally when a large quantity of grain comes on the market: but the artificial hammering of the market by a gang pf irresponsible speculators with the sole object of raking off for themselves a maximum profit is the evil of which we complain, and the nature of this evil is very serious. It is1 not to be wondered at that the elimination of this class of so-called purchasers is urgently demanded by the producer. The only wonderful thing in the situation is that there are still to be found some men who support and defend their retention in the business system of the country. This system of speculation is equally objectionable from the moral point of view. It enables individuals who have no interest in the grain trade hut a gambling interest to draw out of it hundreds or even thousands of dollars for which they have given no value either in grain or in service; and from other individuals it takes hundreds or thousands of dollars for which no value is given-in other words, they are robbed of the money they put into it. It may be serve that it serves them right; they should not be so foolish as to be led into this

game. The answer is that no community has any right to permit in connection with any legitimate business the existence of anything that constitutes a standing temptation to many individuals-a temptation which many of them are unable to resist. The argument in this respect is exactly parallel to that used in connection with the existence of the licensed bar. This was an institution which constituted a standing temptation to many individuals, a temptation under which many of them fell; and the movement for abolition of the bar was strongly supported by the contention that no community had any right to tolerate such a mantrap. As a result the bar has been banished, and, it is to be hoped, permanently.
Numbers of grain men who know the whole grain business say that they would just as soon advise a young man to start the whiskey habit as they would advise him to begin option operations on the Grain Exchange. They claim that these operations were of exactly the same type from a moral point of view as betting on horse racing, and quite as demoralizing ; and the map who begins it is in a fair way to go directly and rapidly to utter ruin. The victim sees somebody clean up in a single deal a few hundred or a thousand dollars. He is convinced there is a good chance of making " easy money." He has no intention of going into it heavily or permanently ; he thinks he can try it for once and he puts in a few dollars. If he loses he tries again. If he wins he is encouraged to make another attempt. He goes in deeper- often he is tempted to use money other than his own and in scores of cases his moral sense is utterly ruined and he is willing to do anything in which there is any hope of getting somebody's money for himself.
Here is an example:-A farmer goes in and expects to help out his income by gathering in a few hundreds or thousands. Instead he loses a few hundreds. He has sense enough to pull out and to keep out, but the inordinate greed of gold and the desire to make up his loss has gripped him hard, and the next thing is he is caught seeking to cheat another farmer out of $*200 on a carload of cattle, his moral sense is so ruined by his experience in grain speculation. Here is another:	A man has run upon
unusually good fortune and cleans up several thousand dollars. He thinks he is satisfied, but the temptation returns. He goes in again and loses all. He is sure he can make it again. He borrows a little here and a little there. He goes in heavily with others' money. There is no come-back. In despair, he turns on the gas jet and ends his life.
A third example: An experienced grain dealer owres a certain firm $50,000. One day he comes into the office and asks for $25,000 more. The firm asks why. He answers that with it he can win back and pay up his debt. After a sleepless night the manager decides to advance it. In a few days the dealer comes back and1 pays in the $75,000; but the firm is wise enough to remark at once, "That is the last money you will have from us." Common report has it that the next gamble of that dealer was in the erection of a provincial parliament building.
Another example: A young man makes $5,000 in land. He is advised that there is a system by which he cannot fail to win out on the Exchange. He studies the system. He is sure it is infallible. He puts in his money and loses it, and is soon anxiously hunting up the Attorney General, who, he expects, will get it back for him. It may be said he wTas a fool; perhaps he was; but that is no reason why toleration should be extended to a species of vicious speculation which exists to ruin just such fools.
A last example: A young farmer came down a few years ago and cleaned up $3,(MM). Visiting at a friend's home he was strongly advised to get away and tamper no more with the business. He declined the advice and in two days lost the whole. He then went home and next season returned with a sum of money in his pocket>
He had decided to risk that amount and no more. He went in and at first lost, but later gathered in some $4,000 or $4,500. Again he plunged, and in a few days went home several hundred dollars in debt.
These are simply a handful of examples out of scores and hundreds which might be cited; and it is the present system of unchecked speculation which makes these examples possible. I wish to say that the system which makes that kind of thing possible, and not only possible but probable and easy for some men, is an outrage on honest business, a foul blot upon twentieth century morality, a monstrous and crying evil that should not be tolerated for a day. I have to say that the man who knowing the necessary concomitance and effects of the system still continues to support and defend it has a code of ethics which is utterly unintelligible from the point of view of square dealing and common business honour. This system of speculation ought to be opposed from every point of view. It has nothing to commend it. It belongs to a condition of things which we should have outgrown. Its spirit is the spirit of the get-rich-quick artist. Its tendency is to belittle and scorn the just methods of regular business. It belongs to the age of the western mining camp and the gambler's den. It forgets that we have entered a new century, with saner ideas, nobler purposes and higher justice. It is a blot on twentieth century business and should be abolished.
I am opposed to it because it seeks to rob the farmer, and what injures the farmer strikes at the well-being of the nation. I am opposed to" it because it tempts men to evil and drives them to ruin. I am opposed to it because I believe nine-tenths of the people of this country are opposed to it. If it could be submitted to a vote of the people-the common, plain-minded honest-purposed people of the country-I am convinced without any suspicion of a doubt that they would banish it absolutely and at once.
The statement is sometimes made that the speculative system does not affect the farmers, and some of the advocates of the system will even go so far as to say that the farmers profit by it. I have already made reference to the fact that the farmer is directly affected by the process of hammering the market in the fall months, and that the farmer who is affected is the farmer who is least able to bear it. In addition to that it should also be mentioned that during the years immediately preceding the stopping of speculation by establishing a fixed price there was a rapid increase in the number of farmers who were getting into the habit of going down to the city and spending weeks or months in hanging round the exchange and participating as free lances in the trading there. There are many who lost and some who gained. The total effect was in no sense advantageous, and the loss in moral deterioration was one to be regretted from every point of view.
The farming population are the losers in the long run both in finance and in morals.

This practice had become very serious some few years ago. Bucket shops were opened in the different towns all through the western provinces; blackboards were put up, and this kind of gambling was carried on. We were able to exert sufficient influence to cause these places to be closed up and the operations to be confined to the Grain Exchange. We hoped that we would be able to eliminate the outside element that was operating in this connection, and thus prevent the masses of the people from being contaminated or endangered by this business. What was the result? Instead of trading out in the country, they came by scores, even by hundreds, to the Grain Exchange, and it was no uncommon thing to look up at the gallery and see them there, with their eye on the blackboard, watching every trade. All this is injurious in its influence and its tendency. These men were not spending their time profitably; they should have been engaged in production; they should have been taking care of their stock and making ready for next year's crop. These practices are a blight on our whole system of trading.
The objection is urged that the elimination of speculation would have the effect of restricting and narrowing the market, that the freedom and facilities of trading would be seriously interfered with. It is said that buyers not having the present freedom of selling would have to buy on a wider margin and the price to the farmer would be lower.
The answer to this question is not far to seek. The market will have all the actual grain that it had before. There will still be all the opportunity for selling that is warranted by the actual grain supply, and so far from being a disadvantage the nearer approach to actuality will make for greater fairness all round, since there will be no fictitious values, fictitious wheat, or fictitious deals, to complicate the situation. The trading will be on the basis of the actual conditions and not on the basis of millions which have no existence. That is the kind of condition and the kind of business which honest men desire for their trading.
As regards the lowering of price necessitated by the narrow market, it is enough to say that the lowering will never be great enough to equal the loss through the hammering of the market which is the constant practice of the speculating class of grain dealers. No grain man of reputation will voice the opinion that a loss of equal magnitude will be incurred
It is possible that with regard to this the position may be taken that has been taken [DOT]before-that it is a very complex matter, and that only the few-those who have been personally in touch with the trade-are qualified to express an opinion. With that view I take direct and unequivocal issue. It is quite true that some phases of the business as it is carried on to-day are obscure and even mysterious ; but it is not true that the general principles of grain dealing are beyond the comprehension of the average man. The principles involved are principles which obtain in

other lines of business. The effects of this undesirable form of trading are abundantly manifest, and the average man has a perfect right to demand that means be taken to avoid and prevent these results. I take the ground that if the transactions are so mysterious that any man cannot pronounce upon them, then the time is ripe for cutting out all the mystery and putting the grain business back on the simple basis of value given for value received.
I wish to present the following as a resolution of the difficulties enunciated and discussed in the remarks I have just presented :
(1)	No person shall hereafter contract or agree, whether orally or in writing, for the sale for future delivery of wheat or any other grain or any product of grain wherein the actual delivery of the commodity sold is not in good faith contemplated or intended by the contracting parties, and any such contract or agreement shall be null and void.
(2)	In any prosecution under this section, evidence that the seller does not have in his possession, actually or potentially, the commodity sold, or that it is contemplated iby the parties-
(a)	that an option only to purchase the commodity is conveyed by the seller ; or
(b)	that from time to time money shall be advanced by the buyer or seller as margins in case of an advance or fall in the market price of the commodity; or
(c)	that settlement, either partial or complete, shall be made by the parties before the time for delivery expires, upon the basis of a payment of the difference between the contract price and the market price of the commodity sold,
shall establish a prima facie case that the contract is in violation of the provisions of subsection one, of this section.
(3)	This section shall not be construed to prohibit the owner, manager, or the duly appointed officer or employee of any elevator of* elevator company, warehouse or mill, or the owner of grain or his agent, from buying or selling grain, or any product thereof, in good faith for future delivery on the open market, to protect purchases or sales made by him or it in the usual or regular course of its business in handling grain, or the products thereof.
(4)	Any person, whether acting individually or as a member of a firm or as an officer or employee of any corporation,. who shall be found guilty of being a party, either directly or indirectly, either as principal, agent, or broker, to any contract made in violation of subsection one hereof shall upon summary conviction be liable to a fine of not less than five hundred dollars, or more than one thousand dollars, and, in default of payment of any such fine, to imprisonment for any term not exceeding six months.
The purpose I have in view is to eliminate that spurious speculation on the grain exchange. I think the argument put forward should convince the average man here that we are not trying to interfere with, but that we are endeavouring to encourage, grain business along every legitimate line, so that the most can be made out of it. As producers of grain, we claim

that these practices that have crept in are injurious to us and are a moral blot on the people of this country.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I am not thoroughly acquainted with the question of the operations of the grain exchange; indeed, the fact of the matter is that my experience has been very limited as regards the operations of any exchange. The hon. member has brought, forward a question that is not a new one, namely, speculative dealing in shares. That question has been raised in every country, I suppose, at one time or another, and frequently legislation has been introduced attempting to control such speculative dealing. I am not very hopeful of that Utopian period ever arriving when you can absolutely prevent speculative dealing in shares on margin or otherwise. In the western country from which my hon. friend comes, I have not the slightest doubt, there are as many men ruined and, perhaps, as many suicides over dealing in land as there have been over dealing in shares on the exchange. Speculation is speculation, no matter what the thing is you are buying or selling. When I say this, however, I do not pretend to say that my hon. friend's argument this evening is not without merit. In the first place, I would be disposed to doubt very much the jurisdiction of this Parliament to prohibit speculative dealing or trading in shares. The fact of the matter is that grave doubt exists as to whether this Parliament had jurisdiction to enact the Grain Act. When you are dealing in shares, whether upon margin or by actual purchase or sale, you are dealing in property, that is, in something which represents title to some property. That, I think, would be a matter which would fall within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. But I have not given it any consideration, .and I am not expressing a definite opinion.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Supposing I were dealing in shares and the shares were represented by a certificate. A certificate must represent value in some way or other. How can you get value for a certificate when you handle 100,000,000 bushels of grain in a day and the total actual grain handled in that day may not amount to more than 10,000,000 bushels?

I suppose if all the purchasing orders on a grain exchange in one day were to be filled, it would be difficult to find the grain, and I presume, on many days that is true. I just want to point out to my hon. friend first that there
is grave doubt as to the jurisdiction of this Parliament to legislate upon the subject. At the moment, speaking offhand, I do not believe we have jurisdiction.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Unless we make it a criminal offence.

subtopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Unless we make it a criminal offence, yes. Dealing in futures in grain has some advantages. For instance, no Canadian miller will go out on the market and sell flour in advance unless he has been able to purchase grain at a certain price covering the period in which he purposes selling his flour. There are certain months of the year in which he cannot buy the actual wheat, and he goes upon the grain exchanges and he buys wheat months ahead at a certain price; and knowing the price the wheat will cost him and the cost of converting that wheat into flour, he can proceed to sell flour to the trade months ahead. If he were not able to do this, that would be a great disadvantage to the miller and possibly a great disadvantage to the public. Furthermore, as my hon. friend has admitted, we have at Winnipeg what is known as " hedging," which is dealing in futures. It takes a great deal of money to handle the grain crop of
Canada from the first of Septem-
9 p.m. ber until the beginning of spring.
I should imagine that the grain dealers in the city of Winnipeg have more than the entire capital of the Canadian banks lent to them at one time or another -probably there would be a peak load, anywhere from $100,060,000 to $150,000,000. This is a very large amount to be involved in trading in grain, and the banks, to protect themselves, insist upon the practice of hedging, which, as I understand it, is this, that every time a customer of a bank sells wheat upon the exchange, he must buy	the same quantity,
and similarly if he buys he must sell. My hon. friend says that is all right. I think it is all right myself, because if this practice did not prevail I do not think the banks would give the credit they do to the grain dealers of Winnipeg, and if the grain dealers of Winnipeg did not get these vast credits it would adversely affect the commercial interests of the country. I fail to see any difference between hedging and speculative buying. I admit that in hedging the intention of the buyer or seller is different from that of the man who is buying or selling shares on margin.
My hon. friend was good enough to mention this matter to me a few. days ago, and



to say that he wished it discussed upon the second reading of this Bill. I then informed him, as I do now, that I should not like to consider his suggestion at the present time, for two reasons: First, I doubt our jurisdiction in the matter, and, secondly, it is extremely doubtful whether it would be wise for us to attempt to legislate upon the subject. At all events, I should not like to commit myself to it without knowing very much more about the matter than I do at the present time, and without giving it a great deal of serious study. I think it would be a very serious matter, indeed, for us to consider legislation of this kind at this time. I am sure the committee appreciates very much, indeed, the motive of my hon. friend in bringing this matter up for consideration, and I have no doubt that hon. gentlemen feel that his contention is not without some merit. However, I do not think it is a fair subject for legislation at . the present time.

Section agreed to.

When the Bill was. in committee the other day I submitted to the Solicitor General the case, for instance, of a child born of a Canadian father in the United States who had become a citizen of that country and who afterwards came back to Canada and was re-naturalized as a British subject. I asked what citizenship the child would have if he came of age while his father was on Canadian soil and a British subject, and the answer was that this case is provided for subsequently. Now I think we should enumerate all possible cases so that there shall be no doubt as to the nationality of a man. I also urged that a certificate of naturalization should not be granted to a man from a couniry under whose laws he could not foreswear allegiance to that country. I cannot see what cases these special certificates are intended to cover. There should be no doubtful cases. We have a law that says under certain conditions a man can become naturalized. When those conditions do not exist he should not become naturalized. I do not think there is

a doubtful case unless it is a political case, that could not be provided for in the law. The conditions should be determined by statute.

speechtext: My hon. friend uses a very broad expression in regard to a statute which is relatively new, when he says it is " the old law.' It is a law of yesterday, but the old law left in the hands of tlhe judiciary the question of naturalization.

speechtext: Before 1915.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Before 1915, and before 1914. In 1913, if I remember well, when the question came up in the House and the Bill was piloted by the present Minister of Justice, strong exception was taken to his departure from very ancient usage. The answer then was that naturalization was, above all things, the gift of the state and that the state ought to be the absolute master of the certificates of citizenship. I well recollect that some hon. gentlemen on both sides, including the late leader of the Liberal party, protested strongly against handing over to hon. ministers of the Crown the power of declaring who should and who should not be British citizens. In reverting to the ancient usage, the old custom of leaving the matter in the hands of a judge
or judges, my hon. friend would not be decreasing the power of the State, because the Government of the country is composed of three elements: the executive, the legislative and the judicial powers. There are some matters which necessarily, by the consensus of opinion, should be in the hands of the judiciary. I might mention a custom which was followed in the old days. My hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) was not then a member of the House, nor was I. His father was before him, and I must say that he was one of the great hopes- of both his party and the country when he was a member of the House of Commons. When my hon. friend's father was a member of the House election cases were fought out before a Committee of the House, and historic cases came before the Controverted Elections Committee. I have one in mind, the famous election of Kamouraska, now represented by our genial friend the present member (Mr. Lapointe). At two or three elections, polls could not be held. The electors were disfranchised by most corrupt machinations, and the late Luc Letellier de St. Just, who was once governor of Quebec, had to protest the election of his opponent, the late Mr. -Chapais. Ac. according to the custom prevailing at that time, the question was handed over to the Elections Committee of the House of Commons. That custom of having controverted elections decided by a Committee of the House had existed in England before and had been adopted in Canada. But soon it was discovered that in a matter of that kin-d, involving hitter political issues, naturally, whatever might be the decision of the Committee, there -would be no satisfaction to either party. I believe both sides of the House will understand why. The Conservatives as well as the Liberals of the day were not satisfied, and by unanimous consent the only wise step was taken in handing over all those election cases to the courts of the land. The Government, or the. State, did not subject itself to any diminution of its power, because the judicial power is an integral part of the power of the State. Since that time all election protests have been decided by the courts of the land instead of by a Committee of the House of Commons. I claim- and I am fortified in my belief by recent events-that by leaving it in the hands of a minister of the Crown who, however respectable and respected he may be, is after all a political creature, to decide whether A, B, or C is entitled to British citizenship is distinctly dangerous and is not in the

interests of the country. On the contrary, it is creating a bias in the minds of unprejudiced people against the authority of the Government to leave in the hands of a political party so important a decision as to whether or not a man is entitled to British citizenship. Therefore, before going any further with this section I think my hon. friend should take the liberal view, and I qualify this by adding, the British view, of this question.
Do not let a political party be the master of the distribution of naturalization papers. My hon. friend, I say it again, used a very broad expression a moment ago to qualify what is an event of very recent date. It was a reactionary measure, and was passed only a few years ago, when the Government took away from the judges of the land the power to grant naturalization certificates. Even though I would seriously question the advisability of doing it, I am ready to admit that during the war the Government might take upon itself the issuance or the non-issuance of naturalization papers; but that has not even been necessary during war time, because all relations with the enemy cease to exist during a period of war. But once peace has been proclaimed, when once the Treaty of Peace is signed, why should the Government take those arbitrary powers unto itself? I urge again on my hon. friend the advisability of thinking this matter over and not taking away from the courts of the land-because that was the old law, that was the ancient usage -that power and transferring it to a minister of the Crown. I urge that without any desire to reflect in any way upon the Secretary of State (Mr. Burrell) who is not only a persona] friend but is respected by both sides of the House, and I think enjoys the confidence of the country. I say to my hon. friend, do not leave such a serious matter, which involves the greatest rights that a citizen can enjoy, in the hands of a politician, respected and respectable as he may be. We should have confidence in the courts of the land. There is no reason whv we should not respect the judiciary. We may, for reasons I have already adduced before the House, question some other important estates of the land, but as regards the judiciary we all respect it. The people have confidence in the judges. Therefore, do not curtail the powers, the ancient powers, of the judiciary with regard to naturalization.

speechtext: No doubt that is why.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
The reason why, I might say, is this,: In the old days, in the province of Ontario, when the administration of provincial affairs was in the hands of gentlemen of the same political faith as hon. gentlemen opposite, I knew of cases where hundreds: of men in my county were taken before a magistrate and were sworn in accordance with the customary oath of allegiance that obtained in Ontario. That magistrate handed them a little slip declaring that they had been properly sworn, and those men believed they were then British subjects, until the advent of this' war, when they found themselves disfranchised and not British subjects as, they believed they were. Now, take other cases. The judges, or some officials who act under the machinery of the courts, are a little lax, for I know of cases in my district, not one but many of them, of men having gone through all the. forms necessary, had sworn the necessary affidavits which had been forwarded to the court officials, and these men were firmly of the opinion that they were properly naturalized. But the matter never went any further, and when, after the passage of the War-Time Elections Act these men applied to the Secretary of State, they found that their naturalization had never been recorded. I tell my hon. friends opposite,, therefore, that I am in favour of this Bill for exactly the opposite reason they thought when I started to speak. I am anxious to protect these men who in good faith attempted to become British subjects, and I believe the taking out of naturalization papers can be worked much more satisfactorily through the Secretary of State or other authority, rather than by court officials who have shown themselves guilty of laxity. They are the men who are responsible for these naturalization proceedings. not being carried to a proper conclusion in the cases I have cited of these men who wrongly believed they were British subjects. I believe this to be a step in the right direction in the interest of the foreigner who is anxious to become a cit-i-

zen oi this country and to become properly naturalized.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
While there may be some force in what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) has said on the general question of submitting such action to the courts,
1	do not believe the question properly arises
under the section we are considering. I do not suppose the provisions of this section would be invoked more than once in twelve months. It is only in cases of doubt, and they would be extremely rare. Especially would the aid of this section probably be invoked where there is litigation as to property, where the rights of inheritance were involved, or something of that kind. When we pass to the general section I have no doubt the criticism in which my hon. friend has indulged might be very properly made. The .hon. gentleman asks:	"Why not adopt
the British system?" Well it has been adopted here, clause by clause, word for word. The clause under discussion is in .clause 4 of the British Act and it is in part
2	of the British Act. The British Act says .that we must adopt part 2 of that Act if our .certificates are to have any force or value .outside of Canada. As I explained upon the last occasion when the Bill was before the committee, one principal idea is to have .a uniform system of naturalization not .only in Great Britain but throughout all the self-governing Dominions. The British Act expressly declares that the British .Parliament cannot, and it does not intend to, in any way abridge the right of selfgoverning Dominions to pass such laws in respect to naturalization as they desire; .but in order to gain recognition for certi-.flcates which we may grant outside of our own territorial jurisdiction, we must comply .with part 2 of the British Act. This clause 4 is exactly word for word the British Act in part 2 of that statute, and if we vary part 2, if we do not abide by its provisions our certificates will not be recognized either .in Great Britain, Australia, South Africa, New Zealand, or Newfoundland. This particular section, I think, will not be invoked, ,as I have already said, more than once in twelve months, perhaps not more than once in five years; but it is in part 2 of .the British Act and it has been put in .part 2 of this Act. We are following a British system in another respect. That system allows the Secretary of State for .Home Affairs to grant the certificates and pass upon them, and we give the same .right to the Secretary of State. In England, this matter no longer goes to the judicial tribunals except in cases which we
.will come to as we proceed, where the Secretary of State is bound to refer the application to the judges for investigation. But in the special cases mentioned undersection 4, the matter is left entirely to the discretion of the Secretary of State.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Is the procedure now entirely changed, and in future must all applications be made direct to the minister, or will the judges pass on the applications as they have done in the past, and then forward them to the Secretary of State?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
The procedure is regulated by section 20. Under the old law you filed your application with the clerk of the court. That was altered five years ago. Now the procedure is laid down by section 20, wrhich provides that:
An alien desiring to 'be naturalized shall apply for a decision establishing that he is qualified and fit to be naturalized under the provisions of this Act to any Judge of any Superior -Court, or to any Judge of any Circuit, District or County Court, and in the North West Territories to such authorities or persons as the Governor in Council may prescribe.
Section 21 provides for posting the application, and the following sections lay down the procedure. The certificate of the judge does no.t now mean the granting of a certificate of naturalization.	The matter goes from	the
judge, after inquiry before the court, to the Secretary of State who actually grants the certificate. Let me emphasize this, because I am told that in a number of counties in the province of Ontario men who have appeared before judicial tribunals, and whose cases have been dealt with and investigated, are of the opinion 'that as soon as the judge has passed upon them they become British subjects to all intents and purposes. That is a mistaken view. They do not become British subjects under this Act until the certificate is actually issued by the Secretary of State.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Has the Secretary of State absolute discretion to grant the certificate or refuse it?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Not in all cases! There are some cases, such as those provided for in section 4, where he has absolute discretion. There is absolute discretion where a man has been seven years removed from British Dominions, or who has not maintained some connection with British Dominions. He has absolute discretion to revoke the certificate in certain other cases, but the granting of the certificate is not in his absolute discretion except in those cases.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The Solicitor General refers to clause 20.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That is the procedure clause.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: If I understand it aright you have to go before a judge who issues a certificate that the applicant is a proper person to become a British subject. Then the Secretary of State issues the certificate of naturalization. But has he to issue it or is it in his discretion to do so or not?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: It is in his absolute discretion.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I would like to inquire of the Solicitor General what application this law will have to the cases of those who are still alien enemies technically, but who will not be alien enemies after the signing of peace. I have in my mind a particular instance that I brought to the attention of the House earlier in the session. In 1917 provision was made by Order in Council for the naturalization of those of alien enemy origin who had lived in. Canada for many years and who could-prove that they were loyal and worthy of citizenship. Provision was made for the naturalization of such people. In the constituency which I represent ninety-three applications were prepared by persons who desired to avail themselves of this provision. They went before the judge, were approved by him in each instance, and the applications were forwarded to the Secretary of State. But for some reason nothing has been done up to this time. The point was made by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) that if this power is placed in the hands of a minister it might be used unfairly. Perhaps he did not put it in that language but that was the inference I drew.
I will point to an instance in which something of that nature took place. These ninety-three people who had made application for naturalization under the Order in Council passed in 1917, were, in nearly every case, men who had lived in Canada for twenty-five, thirty, forty oi[ fifty years. Some of. them had been in Canada even before Confederation and had taken the oath of allegiance. Many of them were actually British subjects but they had no means of proving it; they had no papers, and therefore they were not considered British subjects. These men were not given naturalization under that provision which was made for them. But in one particular instance a bona fide German who had only been for fourteen- or fifteen years a resident 
of Canada and who really did not come under the terms of the Order in Council, was granted naturalization. I am not saying this with any intention of giving offence, but I am perfectly satisfied that the only,reason why he was given his certificate of naturalization was that he had been a supporter of -the Union -Government, and it was for no other reason. I would like to know what the position of these ninety-three people will be. They, to all intents and'purposes, have been- Canadian citizens and British subjects. Their applications were approved by the judge of the county of Waterloo, they have been before the Secretary of State for sixteen months and no action has been taken. What will be the policy of the Government in regard to these applications? The position of these people is similar to another described by an article in the Toronto Globe of to-day and which is as follows:
Owen Sound, June 2S.-One hundred and eight applications for naturalization papers are before Mr. Justice Sutherland here this week. So far, seventy-six cases have been dealt with, and the Judge has not refused his approval in any. Most of the aliens who are applying for Canadian citizenship are of German descent, although three Austrians from Owen Sound and a number of Americans, also have applied. In nearly all instances, the Germans are people who came to Canada from thirty to sixty years ago with their .parents, and were of the belief that their parents had been naturalized, and that they were Canadian citizens, but they found out at the last elections that they had no papers, and are now applying at the first opportunity.
This is practically the case in the constituency I represent. Among these 93 of whom I have spoken some have had sons fighting in France. I would like to know whether they will receive their papers.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
We are going on with this Bill rather irregularly. This question does not arise under section 4 but I have no objection to giving the information row rather than later. Section 8, subsection (b) provides that:
(b) No certificate of naturalization shall, before the expiration of a period of ten years after the termination of the present war, be granted in Canada to any subject of a country which at the time of the passing of this Act was at war with His Majesty.
That is a very clear declaration, and in the case stated by my hon. friend (Mr. Euler), if these persons are of German origin and have not hitherto been naturalized, until a period of ten years elapses after the proclamation of peace, which will be the end of the war, they will not be entitled to naturalization under this Act.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: They will be dead by that time.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
But if they served in
the war, the following subsection excepts .them:
But this provision shall not apply to a person who-
(1)	having served in His Majesty s forces or in the forces of His Majesty's allies or of any country acting in naval or military cooperation with His Majesty was not discharged from such service hy reason of his enemy nationality, sympathy or association; or
(2)	is a member of a race or community known to be opposed to the enemy governments ; or
(3)	was at birth a British subject.
. In any of these cases the prohibition .would not apply; but the man of German descent who has not heretofore been granted a certificate of naturalization will, for ten years after the proclamation of peace, be debarred under this law from obtaining such a certificate.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I protest against any such
law as that. I have stated that these people of whom I speak are, to all intents and purposes, good Ganadians and good British subjects. It seems to me that we :are travelling backward when wq, make the conditions of naturalization so stringent, now that the war is practically over.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
This law was passed in
England in August, 1918. Part 2 has been adopted in this Act, word for word; we have to put it in if it is to apply to Canada.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Well, I protest against the British Act, so far as that is concerned. Surely these men have a good case. Most of them, being fifty, sixty, or seventy years of age, could not possibly have been expected to serve in the war, but some of them had sons in the war. Under this law, through no fault of their own, they .will be precluded for ten years from becoming British subjects. Many of them, I have no doubt, actually are British subjects to-day, but have no proof of it. It should be made easy, rather than difficult, for men who are honest in intention to become citizens of this country.
. Mr. BUREAU:	Would it not be better
to revert to the ancient system of having the application for naturalization papers made to a judge?	[DOT]
, Mr. GUTHRIE:	That would upset the
whole thing. Unless we adopt part 2 of the English Act, our naturalization is no good outside of Canada.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I cannot believe that in order that naturalization papers granted in Canada shall have force and effect all over the British Empire, they must be granted by the .Secretary of .State. W*18^ 's essential to the granting of the application is a fulfilment of the conditions required of the man who wants to become a Canadian citizen, and I do not think the British Government would refuse to recognize our certificate of naturalization if the application was made to a judge and the papers were granted by him instead of by the Secretary of (State. The Act provides that the sufficiency of the evidence may be passed upon by a judge; of course, there is restrictive power in the Secretary of State. There are particular reasons why this matter should be left with the judiciary. The unrest in the country may be said to be caused by the high cost of living, but ii we analyse the conditions we shall find that the unrest is due to the dissatisfaction of the masses with authority-to the lack of respect of the masses for constituted authority. I think that the way to remedy that condition is to take away, as far as possible, from political bodies the power to do those things which can best be done by the judiciary. Of course, although the judiciary command more confidence than a political body, there have been cases which have thrown discredit on the judiciary of this country; I shall discuss that later. But I ask the Solicitor General if he lays down the _ principle that in order to become a British subject throughout the whole of the Empire, it is necessary that the certificate of citizenship should be signed by the Secretary of State instead of by the judge of a Superior or Circuit Court?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I think that the section is well drawn as it is. I cannot conjure up any of the evils which my hon. friend suggests. I do not anticipate that there will be any abuse of the power vested in the Secretary of State; he will toe acting practically in a judicial capacity. Having regard to the plan adopted in Great Britain and to the plan which has been followed here during the last five years, I think it will be wise to adopt the section as it is. We cannot vary it and at the same time give our certificate of naturalization much effect outside of Canada.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That is not my question. I desire to know whether, under the Imperial Act, which we desire to reproduce here, this is one of the essentials?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: This is Part 2, word for word, of the -Imperial Act, and any colony or possession which adopts that part of the English Act may have its certificates of naturalization recognized throughout the United Kingdom and in any other British possession which has similarly adopted Part 2.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Must we adopt Part 2 word for word?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I think there should be nothing more than a necessary variation. In Part 2 of the English Act, the reference to the "Secretary of State for Hbme Affairs" had to be changed, in our reproduction of it, to "Secretary of State of Canada." I should think that we could alter matters of form, but we must maintain the spirit of the Act.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Does the Solicitor General think that it would void the Act if he made a qualification in favour of such people as I have spoken of? Such a course ought to commend itself to the fairness and common sense of the House. An exception should be made in the case of persons who are already British subjects to all intents and purposes; they should not be debarred for ten years from becoming British subjects by naturalization.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That would be a very radical departure from Part 2 of the British Act, which is designed to meet just such cases as my hon. friend has mentioned. If we destroy that part of it, our work will go by the board.
