subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Conditions are different in Canada from those in England. They have not had immigration there such as we have had in the past. While I am not advocating that such exception should apply to those coming into the country in the future, it should apply to those who are already in the country, who came here on invitation and in good faith, who consider themselves British subjects.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The English Act applies to a great many people in England who have been interned during the war and who will be liberated on the proclamation of peace. Many of these people have resided in England for years and were engaged in business there in a large way. Provision is made for just such cases as that., whether in Canada or in the other British Dominions.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I read only tnis afternoon that the United States have adopted the

policy of naturalizing persons who were interned. I am not advocating that we do -that, but I want to show that they follow a more liberal policy.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I have here the Bill adopted by the United States; I think my hon. friend is mistaken as to that.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I also have a copy of the United States Bill, and I am right.

Section agreed to.
On section 5-persons under disability:

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Does this mean that any man who comes from a foreign country and who has children under age must, in order to make those children British subjects, have their names included in his naturalization paper?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
The clause reads:
But any such child may, within one year after attaining his majority, make a declaration of alienage, and shall thereupon cease to be a British subject.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
That is not my point.
Supposing a man goes to the United States and becomes an American citizen, and while he is an American citizen he has children born to him. He comes back to Canada when his children are not twenty-one years of age, and becomes a naturalized British-subject. Is it necessary that the names of those children born in the United States, of an American father, should be mentioned in his certificate?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
That has been the law,
I think, for the last forty years. If children born of a parent in a foreign state or of a parent who is a citizen of that country, who subsequently comes to Canada, those children are alien citizens, and the naturalization of the parent does not affect their status.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: If they are minors?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Yes. But power is given here to mention the children in the certificate obtained by the father, but that does not. bind the children, because when they attain the age of twenty-one years, they have the power to choose.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: It was decided in enforcing the Military Service Act, that a child born in the United States and his parent naturalized, when that child did not make any' declaration to the contrary when he reached the age of twenty-one years, was to be looked upon as a British subject.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
The question was up in the Ontario courts, and the law was laid

down that the child under those circumstances was not a British subject but an alien, but this has been the law in Canada for the last five years-and for the last forty years, I think, though I am not sure.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I think the question of my hon. friend was: If the names of minor children are not included in the certificate of naturalization of the parent, are they British subjects or aliens?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: They are aliens unless they are included in the certificate, under this clause.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
There seems to be an anomaly in the drafting of subclause (1) of this clause which says:
Any such child may, within one year after attaining his majority, make a declaration of alienage, and shall thereupon cease to be a British subject.
Why should the time be limited to one year?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I suppose we must have some limit on the thing, and the presumption is that if within a year he . does not make up his mind adversely, he is a British subject.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I do not insist, but my idea was to leave the question open for any man to make his declaration at any time when he chooses to do so.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Then, perhaps, some
time when we have trouble on our hands, we might find that some of our worthy cilizens would declare that they were no longer British subjects. I hard-10 p.m. ly think that would be fair. If they do not do it within one year, the law is perfectly right in assuming, or presuming, that they were British subjects.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: There were, during the first year of the war, cases where parties attempted to make a declaration of alienage after they had reached twenty-one years, and the Secretary of State refused to accept that declaration of alienage during the war.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Yes. He has a discretion under the clause.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The matter was decided by the English courts in that sense.

Section agreed to.
On section 6-persons previously naturalized :

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: What is the purport of this clause?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The object of the clause is this, that the certificates heretofore issued and signed by judges of the courts would not be accepted in Great Britain or in the other British Dominions; but if a man wants to go abroad and wants something that will give him full rights of British citizenship, he may release his old certificate and ask for a new one.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
That is within the discretion of the Secretary of State? The clause says:
An alien who has been naturalized before the passing of this Act may apply to the Secretary of State for a certificate of naturalization under this Act, and the Secretary of State may grant to him a certificate on such terms and conditions as he may think fit.
The Secretary of State, in his absolute discretion, may refuse.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: He may, and when we come to later clauses, it will be seen that the Secretary of State may revoke certificates on certain conditions.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: There is no way of becoming a citizen unless you are in the good graces of the Secretary of State.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: He is the court of last resort.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-revocation of certificate of naturalization:

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I think this section is open to grave objection, and may cause serious harm. It is true it is based on the Imperial Act of 1918, but it contains something which is not to be found in the Imperial Act. This Bill goes further than the Imperial Act, and even the Imperial Act, as my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) said a few moments ago, was. passed during a terrible war, which saw many enactments which would not be passed in times of peace. First of all, this section gives power to the Secretary of State to revoke a certificate when the citizen has shown himself by act or speech to be disaffected or disloyal to His Majesty. Now that is susceptible of many interpretations. At times certain deeds and certain words have been considered disloyal by some people in this country which I do not believe everybody would admit to be disloyal. For instance, in 1911 it was disloyal, according to some people, for a Canadian citizen to be in favour of reciprocity with the United States. I shall not speak of other occasions, as this one is sufficient to explain what I mean,

Then the Bill does not stipulate the sort of complaint that shall be laid against a man who is liable to revocation of his certificate under this section. Any one can ask the Secretary of State to act. The Secretary of State "shall" in certain cases send a notice to the last known address of the holder of the certificate, giving him an opportunity of claiming that the case be referred to a tribunal of inquiry, which is specified in the following section. The Secretary of State "shall" do that in any case to which subsection 1 or paragraphs (a), (b) or (d) of subsection 2 of this section applies, but in other cases he "may" do it. Even if he does do it, there is no guarantee that the notice has reached the holder of the certificate, and the man will have to incur the expense of applying to a tribunal to be determined by the Secretary of State. That is hardly fair. Moreover, the constitution of that tribunal is not specified except that it shall be presided over by a judge of the Supreme or Exchequer Court, or of any of the Superior Courts. Who will be the other members of that tribunal ? Even if they should be specified, such wide powers should not be given to the Secretary of State. Furthermore, the Imperial Act provided :
Where the Secretary of State is satisfied that a certificate of naturalization granted by him has been obtained by false representations-
And so forth. But this Bill goes further and provides:
That a certificate of naturalization granted by him under this Act, or granted under any Naturalization Act heretofore in force in Canada-
This involves a principle which I believe is unsound. It is retroactive. A man may have obtained a certificate under the law of twenty years ago. The issuing of a certificate to that man twenty years ago effected a contract between him and the Government of His Majesty, and this Parliament has no right to-day to break that contract land say that certificate shall be revoked by virtue of this law. An hon. gentleman behind me says that it would he treating the contract as a scrap of paper. Why have these words " or granted under any Naturalisation Act heretofore in force in Canada " been added in this Bill? That is going further than the Imperial Act. We have no right to annul a certificate granted under a law which was in force in this country twenty years ago. An alien who applies for a certificate under this law will know that he is liable to its pro-
visions, but those who entered into a contract twenty years ago should not be made liable to lose their certificate under this law.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Some days ago when this Bill was before the House, I moved an. amendment dealing with the case of an alien who came from a country whose law was that he could not be fully naturalized in this country. The Solicitor General has in the meantime pointed out to me that the purpose of the Bill before us is practically to standardize naturalization within the British Empire, and that the insertion of the clause which I have moved would interfere with that standardization. Therefore, I am prepared to withdraw the amendment I moved in view of the fact that section 8 provides that no certificate of naturalization shall, before the expiration of a period of ten years after the termination of the present war, be granted in Canada. That will do me till next year, anyway.
Amendment withdrawn.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I most certainly object to paragraph (d) of subsection. 2 of section 7, which reads as follows:
Without prejudice to the foregoing provisions the Secretary of State of Canada may recommend the revocation of a certificate of naturalization granted by him or granted under any Naturalization Act heretofore in force in Canada in any case in which he is satisfied that the person to whom the certificate was granted remains, according to the law of a state at war with His Majesty, a subject of that state.
That means that if the country from which this alien came refuses to recognize a change of status on the part of the applicant, we would refuse to recognize his application to be admitted to British citizenship in this country.
That is to say, the applicant must for all time remain an alien although he resides within our borders. Is that the interpretation which the Solicitor General puts upon the clause?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Clause D is taken word for word from the British Act of 1918. I have no doubt it was framed expressly to meet the case of citizens of any country which recognized dual nationality. It says:
" Remains, according to the law of a state at war with His Majesty, a subject of that state." In that case there is power to revoke his certificate.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Supposing the applicant desires to shed his German or Austrian citizenship? He came away from that country years ago and wishes to have nothing

more to do with it. He wants to know nothing about it and has shaken its dust off his feet. He comes here and wishes to be naturalized as a British citizen. Under this provision he can never become a British citizen and must always remain an alien within our borders.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That would be the effect of the section, and if his country permits dual nationality laws to exist it is deemed in the United Kingdom and in the Dominions that have adopted this law that he should not be naturalized.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: We are dealing with the individual and not with the state from which he came. Germany refuses to recognize the change in allegiance in one of its subjects, although that subject leaves the shores of Germany and, we will say, is not only dissatisfied with conditions in that country, but wishes absolutely to shed his German citizenship, for which purpose he comes here. We are making a contract not with his country, but with the man himself.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend must keep in view the difference between sections 7 and 8. Section 7 provides that in a certain case the man's certificate may be revoked. Section 8, subsection B, provides that if the man is a member of a race or community known to be opposed to the enemy governments he may be naturalized.
Mr. JACOB'S: Take the case of a man coming from Berlin. He is dissatisfied with military autocracy and wishes to come to a country like Canada, where there is freedom, or, rather, where there is supposed to be freedom. He applies for a certificate of naturalization after he has resided here the regulation number of years. The country from which he comes, and which he despises and detests, refuses to recognize his change of allegiance. Is this man who has left the shores of Germany to be bound by this rule which the Empire he now denounces invokes?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That man, in the case stated by my hon. friend, on coming to Canada and residing for the prescribed time can, under section 8, be naturalized. Under section 7, however, his certificate can be revoked.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: We are dealing with the individual.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Under section 7, if he offends his certificate may now be revoked. If he is a German subject coming to Canada he can be naturalized provided he
waits ten years after the proclamation of peace.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Suppose Germany refuses to recognize his change of allegiance?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: If he can show that he is a member of a race or community known to be opposed to enemy governments he can be naturalized.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The minister has apparently drawn the Act with the idea-

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I did not draw it. This is word for word in accordance with the Imperial statute.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: A period of ten years must elapse before a German can be naturalized. Would it not be well to frame the Act so that a man who had been resident in Canada for ten years or more prior to the war could have the privilege of naturalization?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Am I to understand that because this is word for word in accordance with the Imperial Act we shall not have the right to discuss this matter and to see whether it is advisable or not that we should swallow it bolus bolus? I think that this Act will open the door to fraud and will bring dishonour on many a family in Canada. You say that you can cancel the certificate because at the time it was obtained a man was not of good character. We have seen in this country of late conspiracies against individuals, whereby affidavits and declarations have been made which have been proven subsequently to be false, in an attempt to ruin men. A man may have striven hard to raise his family and somebody may have a grudge against him. He is away from Canada and a charge is made against him. A registered notice is sent to his last address and he does not receive it, and on the charge of a lot of scoundrels far worse than himself a judgment is passed on him. The evidence is there, of course, because nothing can be done but to accept it, and his certificate is cancelled. This provision, I repeat, opens the door to fraud, and I for one will not accept as a satisfactory answer the assertion that it is the same as the Imperial Act. Are we under any obligation blindly to accept the Imperial Act? We are here to legislate for ourselves, and what valid reason is there why we should not? Where is the responsibility of the people who sit here if we are to have the laws of our neighbours copied in their entirety without our having the right to discuss or analyse them? Are we simply to be told " This is the Imperial Act and we can do no

more?" If in order to be a citizen of the British Empire you must have the Imperial Act, very well. But if we think that the naturalization laws of Canada-not of the British Empire but of Canada-are not satisfactory, then let the people of Canada have laws to suit themselves; and he who wants to be a citizen of the British Empire may have this Act. But if you want a law for Canada we must discuss every single proviso of that law and every section of it and have the explanation as to the why and wherefore of that lavr. Conditions in Britain may be different from those in Canada, and as my hon. friend from Kam-ouraska (Mr. Lapointe) said just now this law was passed in England in 1918. In 1918 and during the war we know in what state the peoples of the various countries were. We know that people were not acting as they had acted three or four years before, or will act three or four years hereafter. Another objection which I must voice is in regard to the exercise of this much-heard-of " absolute authority." Why the word " absolute?" We have had too much absolutism in this country, and I do not believe that these words " absolute authority " should appear in any section of our statutes. Sir, this " absolute " authority is the cause of the discontent and unrest in this country. It is this " absolute " authority and the manner in which it is exercised that has made the people lose confidence in the rulers of the country today, and I for one am not ready to accept this section, against which I must register my emphatic protest, unless very convincing and satisfactory explanations are forthcoming.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I move that we strike
out paragraph (d) of subsection 2 of section 7 which reads: "remains, according to the law of a state at war with His Majesty, a subject of that state."

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I am afraid I cannot
accept that amendment. If we do it will be a radical departure, and I am afraid the whole Bill will be involved. There is no disposition on the part of any one to choke off discussion. We desire the fullest discussion, and I quite agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) that it is not necessary always to follow Imperial enactments.
If you are going to have an Imperial naturalization law, you must take this enactment. If the House does not deem it well to have the Imperial law upon the subject, it may depart from it, because the Imperial Government has been very careful in framing the statute to say that the 	,	,
dominions shall have authority to pass such laws as they see fit, but those laws will not be accepted in other parts of the Empire unless we adopt part 2. As the section in question is a portion of part 2 of the Imperial Act, I think it will be the judgment of the House that it should be adopted as it stands.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that we shall have to adopt all the amendments that may be imade to the Imperial Act in order to have British naturalization?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: We have to adopt all of part 2 of our Act.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
That was
passed last year only.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: It was passed last year as an amendment to the Act of 1914 and the two are to be read together.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Then we shall have to. adopt all the amendments which may be passed to part 2 in order to retain the rights we have to British naturalization?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I do not say word for word. I say we are not entitled to make any radical change if we desire our certificates-to have any effect outside of Canada.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I prefer retaining my rights in the matter of autonomy.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Now, let us look at section 7, subsection (I):
It provides that where the Secretary of State of Canada is satisfied that a certificate of naturalization granted by him under this Act, oY granted under any Naturalization Act heretofore in force in Canada, has been obtained (1) by false representations or by fraud, or by concealment of material facts which involves fraud, he may recommend to the Governor General a revocation of that certificate. Will the House not agree that in a case of that kind there should be a revocation of the certificate?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That is all right.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: What about the last part of that paragraph?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The certificate mav be revoked by the Governor in Council.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: My hon. friend should continue his reading, he has not read the worst part of the paragraph.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I will go on with the balance of the section:

-or that the person to whom the certificate is granted has shown himself by act or speech to be disaffected or disloyal to His Majesty

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That is a matter of proof to be determined by the courts, not the Secretary of State.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: -"has shown himself disaffected or disloyal to His Majesty." Is the House with me that that is good ground for the revocation of the certificate?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: It is.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Then we are agreed so far. The paragraph goes on:
The Secretary of State may recommend that the certificate be revoked and the Governor in Council may by order revoke the same accordingly.
The Secretary of State does not do it. The Government of Canada revokes the certificate and will have to accept the responsibility.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That is what we object to.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
That applies to cases only of false representations or fraud, concealment of material facts, or acts or speeches of disloyalty. Now let us come to subsection 2:
Without prejudice to the foregoing provisions the Secretary of State of Canada may recommend the revocation of a certificate of naturalization granted by him-
Now these words are not in the British Act:
or granted under any Naturalization Act heretofore in force in Canada in any case in which he is satisfied that the person to whom the certificate was granted either-
Here are the cases:
(a) has, during any war in which His Majesty is engaged, unlawfully traded or communicated with the enemy or with the subject of any enemy state, or been engaged in or associated with any business which is to his knowledge carried on in such manner as to assist the enemy in such war; or-
I think the House will agree with me that is good ground for the revocation of a certificate. I proceed with the quotation:
- (b) was not of good character at the date of the grant of the certificate.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: We will oppose that.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I submit to the House
that is very good ground for revoking the certificate. In fact

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
It is better ground for
political trickery.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: -the House unanimously a few days ago, and with very little debate, said it was ground for deportation.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Suppose a man has been in the habit of beating horses?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I would not say that
man was a man of bad character exactly. I think the language is capable of reasonable interpretation and it will be reasonably interpreted.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
There is a doubt about
that, a very grave one.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Now let us go to paragraph (c): Under it the Secretary of State has power to revoke the certificate of a man who, being a British subject, leaves the British dominions and stays away for seven years, and does not maintain any connection therewith. I should think we could take it for granted that that man should be struck off the list. In such a case the Secretary of State may strike him off or revoke his certificate.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I think it can be assumed that a man who has been away from Canada, or a British possession, for seven years and has not maintained any connection with this country or any British possession, is of very little use as a citizen.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: If he came back with a million we would find him very useful.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: We would not strike him off if he was a very useful citizen. The Secretary of State would use ordinary discretion in such matters.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: If he were on the right side of politics.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That is only an inference on the part of my hon. friend, who would probably act in such a way if he had the power.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
We know others iwho
would do it now.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
It was not done in this country under the Union Government. Now we will take subsection (d):	.
remains, according to the law of the state at war with His Majesty, a subject of that state.
I do not want to repeat what I said before, but the effect of that section is merely this: That certificate of nationality of the subject, residing in Canada, of any state in which there is the law of dual nationality

is subject to revocation if we are at war with that state.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Does that apply to Russia?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I do not know whether the law of dual nationality obtains in Russia, I believe there is such a .law in Germany and Austria.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Is there not such a law in France?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I am not sure as to that. If that were the case, and if we were at war *with France, that man's certificate could be revoked under this section.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Does that mean that any Canadian citizen of German nationality who is naturalized in Canada may have his certificate revoked?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I think that is what it means.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That is wholesale revocation.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I think a citizen residing in this country, coming originally from Germany where the law of dual nationality is in force, and a country at war with His Majesty, would have his certificate revoked.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Have such persons no right to make an option?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Under paragraphs (a), (b), (c) and (d), which I have just read, there may be a judicial inquiry. I think every safeguard is offered to the holder of the certificate, and he can feel reasonably sure that his certificate will not be revoked without good grounds.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The law is there.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: My hon. friend/ from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) points out that this section was part of the Imperial Act of 1918, which was passed as a war measure. It was certainly passed during the war, and I have no doubt in my own mind that when it was drafted and passed by the Imperial Parliament it was intended to be active in its operation for at least ten years after the war, because it expressly states that no certificate shall be granted in any part of the Empire until ten years after the war has ceased, to the subject of a country which has been at war with Great Britain.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: When was that law passed?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
It was passed in the month of August, 1918. The original Act
[Mr. Gufihirie.l
was passed in Great Britain on the 4th or 7th day of August, 1914, a day or two after the declaration of war. It was amended in August, 1918, and section 7 of the Bill now before the House seeks, as far as possible, to conform word for word with the enactment in the Imperial statute. Now it comes back to the question which I mentioned before.
In the opinion of the House, should we have a uniform naturalization law, one which will apply in Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Newfoundland? If the House deems it proper to have such a law, we must pass this section or we do not comply with part 2 of the British Act.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Why have these
words been added to the Canadian law?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The words have been added obviously to cover the case of every certificate heretofore granted.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That has not been done by the British Parliament.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The British Act says "under this Act," meaning the Acts of 1918 and of 1914 because they are to be read together.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Why not leave our local Naturalization Act alone?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: This applies to all laws hitherto in force.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Why?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: To make it as broad as we possibly can.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Retroactive-"a
scrap of paper."

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister if the Imperial Act of 1914 prohibits naturalization for ten years.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: No, it is the Act of 1918 which prohibits that.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: What are the benefits of Imperial naturalization and how many of our citizens would be likely to reap any of them? I am a good Imperialist, but honestly I want to say to 'this committee that naturalization in Canada will pretty nearly do me for my time.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
That might be so but there are others, I suppose, who might some day remove from Canada and go to some other British possession throughout the world or to the United Kingdom itself. If citizenship is of value at all, and I have always understood that British citizenship

was of great value, it is worth making secure.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: In my case Canadian citizenship carries with it British citizenship.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: My hon. friend is under the impression that his statement is correct but it is not correct; citizenship in Canada is limited territorially to Canada.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Why disturb that Act? Why not let us have local naturalization?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The object of passing a new Act is that Canadian citizenship shall be good in any part of the world under the British flag.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Who asked for it?
v Mr. JACOBS: Why not let us have two Acts and then we will not complain.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I am in the judgment of the House on that point. My own opinion, and the Government's opinion, is that it is very desirable to have a uniform law in regard to naturalization throughout the Empire. For that reason the Bill is now before the House.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I should like to make myself clear on that point. I see no objection to having what may be termed Imperial citizenship but I do see an objection to making it more difficult to get Canadian citizenship now than it was before the war for the purpose of getting a wider application of Canadian citizenship.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: My hon. friend is a British citizen throughout the world now, but many people who have obtained citizenship in this country are only British subjects until they reach the three-mile limit outside the shores of Canada. A situation might arise which would be very difficult for a Canadian citizen.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: What are they outside of the shores of Canada, Canadians?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: A naturalized Canadian under the present law might enlist in a Canadian force, might go to fight the battles of the Empire in Europe and might be taken prisoner. He would not be treated as a prisoner. If taken by the country which he had left, he would be treated as a deserter and shot. He would have no rights of citizenship in Great Britain and no rights at all outside of Canada.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: He is not a British subject?	* j

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I suppose one could
enumerate many cases where British citizenship would be of the greatest advantage to an individual. The object throughout the Empire is, as far as possible, to obtain uniformity and there is no doubt that the abject of some of the drastic amendments passed by the Imperial House in August last was, as far as possible to see to it by legislation that improper persons should by no means whatever obtain British citizenship. That was done for the future safety of the State and it is to carry out that purpose that his Bill is now introduced.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Under paragraph (c) of section 7, what becomes of a person who has been resident in the United States for a number of years, who has never taken out naturalization papers there but who was born in Canada?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That man will continue to be a British subject.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The minister said that the ten-year period did not apply to Great Britain under the Imperial Act. What period does apply?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend misunderstood me. Under the Imperial Act a five-year residence is necessary. That has been out law for Canada. The provision of this Bill is that:
No certificate of naturalization shall, before the expiration of a period of ten years after the termination of the present war, be granted in Canada to any subject of a country which at the time of the passing of this Act was at war with His Majesty.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That is not in the Imperial Act?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Yes, word for word.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I am sure the Committee fully realize the real meaning of the words of the Solicitor General. It is a great privilege to be able to grant a certificate of naturalization which will apply to the whole British Empire, but my hon. friend says that every time the British Parliament shall make the slightest change in the Imperial Act we, the Canadian Parliament, shall have to effect the same change, following theirs, in order that our certificates shall be available throughout the British Empire. That is one of the greatest sacrifices of autonomy that we were ever asked to make. We bind ourselves to make the same change every time. I do not think this is a fair policy for this country to adopt. But apart from that, I come back to the

objection I made to these words which were added to the Imperial Act. The British Parliament, in the course of the war, passed this Imperial Act which provides for the revocation of naturalization certificates. That did not exist in the British law formerly, but it was done during the war, to meet conditions which arose on account of the war. We are to-day enacting similar legislation, but we are making it a good deal more drastic than the British law is because we are giving it a retroactive effect. The British Act gives power to revoke certificates which may be issued under the Act of 1918. But here in this country this Government asks the power to revoke not only a certificate granted by the Secretary of State under this Act, but certificates granted under any naturalization Act heretofore in force in Canada. A man who was naturalized twenty years ago under the Canadian law as it existed then, -who has a certificate, which ds a contract entered into between him and His Majesty, is liable to have his certificate cancelled, his contract revoked, at the will and behest of the officials of this Government. I protest against this iaw and especially against the addition to the Imperial Act of the words to which I have referred. I move that section 7 be struck out.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
The Solicitor General has given no reason why these words should be added. When the British Act was passed in 1918 the war was in progress, the Germans were conducting an elaborate spy system; efforts were being made by persons of enemy natrons to gain access to England; all sorts of pretenses and fajse oaths were being made by those who were desirous of securing naturalization papers. But although the war is practically over we are now providing that a certificate obtained twenty years ago may be cancelled because it was obtained by a man not of " good character." This opens the door to all sorts of frauds. The Solicitor General knows that retroactive law is considered to be immoral. A man's citizenship is one of his most priceless possessions. Either the Solicitor General has some idea of holding this provision over certain citizens as a threat-
I do not say that he has-or he has some information to justify this provision which he does not wish to disclose.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: We are at least entitled to an explanation as to why these words were added.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I have already explained that it is to make the Act broad enough to

coveT all cases in Canada of persons who obtained their certificates under the conditions set out in clause 7. If they obtained them by fraud, misrepresentation or concealment, or if they have been guilty of disloyalty, no matter when the certificates were issued, they are liable to be cancelled.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Has the Solicitor General had any complaints about certificates which were granted under the old Naturalization Act, and if so, how many?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: In some parts of Canada there may be certain persons who claim the rights of Canadian citizenship but whose conduct during the last eight or nine weeks has been very questionable. These persons may have obtained their certificates ten, fifteen, or twenty years ago. I for one do not desire to protect them; I would make therfi liable to this law.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
A committee of this
House has had under consideration a revision of the Criminal Code in order to provide for cases of sedition, disloyalty, and so on. We have the spectacle that in the absence of any report from that committee, or any legislation based upon it, men who, it is alleged, have acted disloyally, or been accused of sedition have been arrested. Either we are able to legislate to maintain order in this country, or we are not. If we are not, we ought to abdicate as a Parliament; if we are, we ought not to leave it in the hands of one man, a member of a political body, to determine whether or not a man -who is a citizen of this country by virtue of a contract entered into with His Majesty shall continue so to be. If there is anything in the conduct of a citizen which endangers the safety of the public or jeopardizes law and order and good government, we have the power to legislate to meet that condition. If a man who twenty years ago received a certificate of naturalization is guilty of treason or of sedition, punish him accordingly; but do not leave to the Secretary of State the power to revoke his certificate at will. I say " at will," because when the head of a department, who is the person most familiar with the conditions in that department, makes a recommendation to the Governor in Council, that recommendation is generally accepted. What I do object to is that power be given to one man to revoke a certificate that was granted twenty or thirty years ago; that is not conducive to good order among the people or to confidence in the Govern-

ment. If a body of men, absolutely independent of political influence had to deal with such certificates, I might not have so much objection. The minister says that the Act has been so worded as to make it broad enough to cover the ground; he goes on to cite a case in which he would cancel certificates, and hon. gentlemen opposite applaud. We are not here to talk sentiment; we are not here to wave the flag; we are here to legislate, not under war conditions, but on the eve of peace; and to legislate with a view to bringing contentment to the people. I have said that the unrest in Canada is due mostly to the fact that the masses of the people have no cer-fidence in the Government or in Governments generally; they say to themselves: We will have to take the law in our own hands. That is one of the causes of the unrest; for God's sake, don't go any further; don't be autocratic. We do not want any Kaiserism in this country; we have fought to put it down. England was close to the enemy and knew what her requirements were when she passed this Act; why should we go further? I do not think any such provision is justifiable, and I shall not vote for it.	.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: My hon. friend is obviously under a misapprehension as to the effect of this section. He said that he would not have so much objection if the matter were not in the hands of a political body; if there was judicial investigation.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I said I would have less objection.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The Solicitor General has already pointed out that neither the Secretary of State nor the Governor in Council has any power to revoke certificates under these conditions without the holding of a judicial investigation where the person concerned desires it.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: My objection was to the principle involved in granting this power to the Secretary of State, but I make no exception to any powers when I say that certificates granted under any naturalization law heretofore existing ought not to be cancelled either by a political or by a judicial body.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Let me take up the three points raised by my hon.. friend. The certificates cannot be revoked except after a judicial investigation and a finding of a judicial body upon them. That is number one.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: By a commission named by Order in Council. The commissioners would be named by the Government.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Which commission must be presided over by a judge.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: And the summons served by mail.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: It may be the superior court of a province, or a commission presided oveT by a judge, but it must be a judicial investigation. Then, number two -my hon. friend will recall the fact that in Great Britain they have had a uniform naturalization law for many years under which a five-year period of residence is required before naturalization. We had in Canada our own naturalization law which required a three-year period. In 1911, at the Imperial Conference, at which Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his then Liberal colleagues were present, it was unanimously decided that we should have a uniform naturalization law throughout the Empire, and that uniform law has now come into effect; it was passed in Great Britain in 1914, and passed by this House, I think, in the same year. That law, as regards Great Britain, continued the provision of five years' residence. As regards Canada, it provided a new basis for naturalization which gave citizenship throughout the whole Empire.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Was that to abrogate our three-year period?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: It has. Had we seen fit, we could have continued a dual system of having a Canadian naturalization law for naturalization only in Canada and we could have adopted the general Imperial law under which Imperial citizenship might have been obtained. The Parliament of Canada decided to adopt the general Imperial law with a five-year residence. As my hon. friend the Solicitor General has pointed out, when you come to this law, if the wording had been simply to revoke any certificate of naturalization granted under this Bill, no certificate could have been- revoked except the few that have been granted under the five-year Act, which has been in force in this country for only a year or two. Therefore, if you are to deal with revocation certificates of Canadian naturalization you must make provision for doing so in this Act.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: You want wholesale quantities.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
The particular amendment upon which the vote is being taken



is to strike out subclause (d) of this clause. What is the position with reference to this amendment? If a man is a citizen of a foreign country and he becomes naturalized in this, and by the law of that foreign country he still continues a citizen of that country, even although naturalized in this, then if war breaks out between the two countries, while that war is on, his certificate of naturalization may be revoked.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Under those clauses he could be interned. This British subject of yesterday could be interned to-morrow.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: He could not be interned until after his certificate was revoked.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Precisely.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Let us look at the situation frankly and consider it, because this was considered by the Imperial Government and by other Governments of the Empire. If a man is a citizen of another country, we cannot change that fact, and if we are at war with that country and if he is liable to military service in that country, if he is liable ta be shot as a traitor if he goes out of this country because we ask him to render some service, is it not a reasonable thing that when the war is actually on, when we are actually making war against that country, we
11 p.m. should revoke his certificate here? It is not our fault that he is a citizen of the other country; we cannot help ourselves; the country of his origin makes that so. All that this is intended to do is to cover that case. If war is not on, it does not apply. The clause says, " at war." Let me read the clause:
Remains, according- to the law of a state at war with His Majesty, a subject of that State.
It is only during the period of the war that this right of revocation exists. I submit that provision embodied in the Imperial Act, which is designed to preserve uniformity throughout the Empire, is not an unreasonable one, and is not such a one as should induce us to reject the Imperial Act in favour of creating a separate Canadian nationality.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: This is just a contingent citizenship, depending upon peace. The moment war comes, here is a man whose certificate you can cancel, and as the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) said, if he is deported, he may be shot. That is what you call giving dignity to the citizenship of a country. I do not view the matter in that light.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Shot by his own people.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: You abandon him as a derelict.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
The question of dual
nationality is one presenting very grave difficulties and one upon which the Imperial Conference did not reach an agreement. Many thought we should not naturalize a man who by the law of his own country continued to be a citizen of that country. The conference did not agree to do that; so that dual nationality continues but if war broke out between the two States involved, then under certain conditions, naturalization might be revoked.
Mr. JACOB'S:	He might be called a
" fair weather " British subject.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I have not succeeded in getting an explanation from the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) as regards the words added to the Imperial Act. I have been asking for an explanation, and, I am trying to get it from the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) now. We are basing our legislation on the Imperial Act. We say that in order to get the benefit of British naturalization, we must have the same enactment as the Imperial Parliament has. Why should we add this retroactive clause which is most arbitrary? It is Prussian in its spirit; it is unworthy of the Dominion of Canada, and it is those words especially to which I object and which I want to have struck off from the clause.
Amendment (Mr. Jacobs) negatived.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I move to amend
clause 7 by striking out from the said clause in the 45th line on page three of the Bill, the following words:
Under this Act, or granted under any Naturalization Act heretofore in force in Canada.
Amendment negatived; yeas., 39; nays, 58.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I should like a little information with regard to paragraph (b) of subsection 2, which provides for the revocation of certificate where the applicant was not of good character at the time of granting the certificate. Suppose that ten or fifteen years after the granting of a certificate it is found out that the applicant was not of good character at the time the certificate was issued, but in the meantime has reformed and become a good citizen?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That is where the political game comes in.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: In the cases mentioned in paragraphs (a), (b) and (d), a judicial inquiry must be held-

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: A McLennan inquiry.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: -presided over by one who is or has been a judge of the Supreme or Exchequer Court or of a Superior Court of a province, and the inquiry shall be conducted in such manner as the Governor in Council shall direct.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: How is the man summoned before that inquiry?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The rules of court of, the province apply.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Subsection 3 provides that the summons shall be by notice given or sent to the last known address of the holder of the certificate. That is not the, rules of court. The man may have left that address and may never receive the notice, but the trial would go on and the certificate be revoked.

Section agreed to.
On section 8-effect of revocation certificate of naturalization.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Do I understand that under subsection 1 a natural-born British subject would be subject to the order of the Secretary of State?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: A natural-born British subject does not have a certificate. This only applies to persons who have a certificate.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Paragraph (b) says:
In the case of a wife who was at birth a British subject, unless he is satisfied that if she had held a certificate of naturalization in her own right, the certificate could properly have been revoked under this Act.
That certainly applies to a British-born subject.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That is the wife.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: A woman can be a British subject by birth as well as a man, and under this section an order can be made that she shall no longer be a British subject.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I think the meaning oi the section is this: A woman who was by birth a British subject loses her nationality by marriage to a man who was not a British subject, but an order shall not be made in her case "unless he is satisfied that if she had held a certificate of naturalization in her own right the certificate could properly have been revoked under this Act, and the provisions of this Act as to referring cases for inquiry shall apply to the making of any such order as they apply to the revocation of a certificate." A case of
that kind would be a case for inquiry and would have to be referred to the judge. The word "he" at the end of line 36 should be "the Governor in Council," and I move to amend the section accordingly.
Amendment agreed to.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: What is the meaning ol subsection 2?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I do not know that I can make it any clearer. It is the governing section and will have effect in substitution for any other provisions of this Act as to the effect upon the wife and children of any person where the person ceases to be a British subject. There is an omission in subsection 3 which I wish to remedy. An Act was passed by this House as an amendment to the Immigration Act, providing that under certain conditions British subjects may be deported from Canada, but it does not apply to British subjects who have become such by naturalization. To give this Act effect in regard to British subjects who have become such by naturalization I beg to move that the following words be added to subsection 3 of section 8:
and shall thereafter for the purposes of this Act and of the Immigration Act be deemed never to have been naturalized.
The objection has been taken that a British subject, under the amendment to the Immigration Act, can be deported under certain conditions but the person who has been naturalized and whose certificate is revoked perhaps could not, the natural-born British subject being in an adverse position in that respect.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I do not know that we should mix up the Immigration Act with this. This provides that where a certificate of naturalization is revoked the former holder shall be regarded as an alien and as a subject of the State to which he belonged at the time the certificate was granted. Now, take an American citizen coming here and forswearing his allegiance to the United States. The moment he takes the oath of allegiance here and becomes a Canadian citizen he ceases to be an American citizen. How can we legislate him back to citizenship of the United States?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
The Immigration Act passed this session-the short Act passed a week or ten days ago-applies to British subjects by birth and provides that under certain conditions they may be deported from Canada, but it would have no application to a naturalized subject whose certificate was revoked. Subsection I of sec-

tidh 15 of the Immigration Act provides that that section in that Act shall not apply to any person who is a British subject either by reason of birth in Canada or by reason of naturalization in Canada. So that the naturalized subject could not be deported under the Immigration Act. Now, the naturalized subject whose certificate is revoked should surely not be in a better position than the British subject born in the United Kingdom, and the intention is to obviate this inequality. You cannot deport a man born or naturalized in Canada, but you can, under the Immigration Act, under certain conditions deport a British subject born in the United Kingdom. The object is to place the alien who has been naturalized in the same position as the person born in the United Kingdom. He otherwise could say: I come within the exception in the Immigration Act; I was naturalized in Canada and the Immigration Act does not apply to me.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I would rather amend the Immigration Act.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That was considered, and possibly it might have been the better course. But the Immigration Act has been assented to and it would be far more convenient to make the provision in this.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I think we should let this stand until next year. No great harm wpuld be done, and it would be better than burdening the Naturalization Act with what I might call a side clause. I do not think we should mix that Act with the Immigration Act, I want to draw the ministr's attention to subsection 3 of section 8, which reads:
Where a certificate of naturalization is revoked the former holder thereof shall be regarded as an alien and as a subject of the state to which he belonged at the time the certificate was granted.
What is the object of that?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: He will revert to his original citizenship. I can see the hon. member's point with regard to mixing the two Acts, but it would be rather a serious thing to permit our law to remain, even until next year, in the condition in which it would be if we did not adopt this amendment. It would be said: You can deport from the country a British subject born in the United Kingdom and cannot an alien whose conduct deprives him of the right to his certificate. The only way by which the anomaly can be overcome is by the amendment.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: You declare the man shall belong to the country from which he came. Suppose the law in that country provides that as soon as one of its citizens forswears his allegiance to that country he shall cease to be its subject?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: We will have to take that chance.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: We cannot legislate a man into citizenship of the United States, and where will you deport him?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: He would be considered to be a citizen of the country to which he belonged prior to naturalization.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: But I want to know where you will deport him. May I ask, in regard to subsection 4 (a), are we still at war with the various enemy countries, notwithstanding the armistice?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: We are at war until the proclamation of peace by this Government and the Imperial Government. The signing of the Peace Treaty does not end the war until there is a proclamation by these Governments.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: What about Russia at the present moment? Are we considered at war with that country?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: We never have been at war with Russia.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Just fighting Russia without being at war?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: This subsection means that persons who have been citizens of this country for forty or fifty years will be obliged to reside in Canada for ten years more before they can take advantage of this Act. Is that so?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Yes, if their country oi origin is one that has been at war with His Majesty.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
This is absolutely unfair and unreasonable. Do be fair in a matter of this kind. I know hundreds, yes thousands, of citizens in this country who have lived here for forty or fifty years and have been good Canadians, in every sense as good as any hon. gentleman in this House, I care not who he may be. They have paid their way and have contributed to the finances of the country in many ways. They have served in prominent positions, have been elected to different offices in the gift of the country, and have voted all these years. A great many of them have sent sons over to France, who are buried there,

sons killed in the defence of this country. Do you mean to say that it is reasonable or fair to require men of this class to reside ten years longer in Canada before they can become naturalized? This is shameful legislation.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That brings us back to the discussion that took place an hour or two ago. We cannot depart from this language without a radical change from the Imperial Act, probably upsetting all the provisions we have passed. We have followed the Imperial Act and, probably in accordance with legislation in the Colonies -although I am not absolutely certain of this-this clause was drafted; and, I submit, it is fair.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: Surely you do not contend that.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
In my judgment it is fair that for the next ten years citizens originating from countries at war with His Majesty at the present time should be put on a term of probation. There is a provision here that if they have fought' on behalf of the Allies in the war they are entitled to obtain certificates. Or if the person is a member of a race or community known to be opposed to the enemy governments, he is entitled to obtain a certificate. But if they are subjects of Germany or Austria, and are not opposed to the enemy governments, then they cannot obtain certificates of naturalization throughout the British Empire for a period of ten years.
Mr. PEDLOW7: What better evidence could we ask regarding the position of men from enemy countries than the fact that these men have fought against the countries to which they formerly owed allegiance, that not only they but their sons have fought and died on behalf of Canada? What better evidence should we want or need than that?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: There is nothing in the Act to say that that is not good evidence. They are entitled to give that evidence if they want to.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I would like to ask the Solicitor General or any member of the Government regarding the position of homesteaders in the three western provinces. This legislation affects thousands of people who came to Canada and settled under the Homestead Act prior to 1914. These men have homesteaded their land; they have been on it ever since they came to the country, and have earned their homesteads.
Of course they could not take out naturalization papers during the war, but they have entered into an agreement with the Government and they have fulfilled their part of the contract. Will the Government expect these men, many of whom are old people, to stay for another ten years on those homesteads without getting their land?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: This Bill has nothing to do with the right to hold land.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: No, but these people have earned their land and they cannot get their patents until they are naturalized.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: I did not know that there was such a provision.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: The conditions in regard to a homestead entry are that a man must live three years on the land and make certain improvements on it. Take the case of a man who arrives in the country and goes on the land. He is not naturalized but while he is earning a living and putting in his time making improvements, he is qualifying for citizenship. Such a man^ has been debarred for the last seven years from making application for a patent. Will that man now have to wait ten years longer?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I confess' I was not
aware of any condition that a man in order to obtain a. patent had to be a British subject.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: He has to be before he can get his patent.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: He has to be a British subject before getting his patent?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: On the form of application for a patent the question appears: "Are you a British subject by birth or naturalization?"

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: That may be, but is there anything in our Land Act which says he shall not get the patent unless he is a British subject?

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext: There is.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
If there is such a provision I was not aware of it. In that case, under this section, the man would have to wait for ten years from the end of the war before he could get a certificate of naturalization. It might be that an amendment could be made to the Lands Act to meet such a case. It looks to me as being a little unreasonable, because there is a special provision in this Bill, a saving clause, that aliens shall be entitled to hold property-

to own, sell, or inherit it-they have all the rights in regard to property of British subjects.
Mr. W. II. WHITE: They have such rights if they purchase the land, but not in the case of a free grant.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
The clause is very explicit; they have all the rights of British subjects in regard to property. If my hon. friend's contention is right it might become necessary in the future to amend the Dominion Lands Act, because I think it would be quite reasonable that a man who has done his work, made his improvements and fulfilled the conditions ought to get his patent. I do not know why he should not.
iMr. DAVIS: I am quite sure that the hon. member (Mr. W. H. White) is absolutely right, that the entrant may make entry before having obtained naturalization, but he cannot obtain his patent until he is naturalized. There are many cases throughout Western Canada where a man has spent six, seven, eight, or nine years upon his ,,land already, and this enactment we are considering means that he must wait ten years longer in order to get the patent for that land. Now I know of Polanders who sent their sons to the war, telling them that if they did not go they would not be considered good Canadians when the war was over, that it was their place to take their stand with Canadian young men. Yet men in that position, because the district in Poland from which they came is part of Germany, would now be debarred for ten years more, after having been here perhaps nine years, from having their homesteads granted to them. I think it is perfectly proper to make the provisions of our law harmonize vvith those of Great Britain, there would be advantages in that to Canada. But in certain special cases I think provision should be made such as would enable men of the class that I have described to obtain their patents.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I have already spoken on this subject and I realize the possible disability under which I am with regard to making the plea I am going to make and which refers to the people of whom I spoke before. I am going to offer an amendment to the clause. Under the- clause as it is drafted it will be possible for subjects of enemy countries to become citizens of Canada only after an additional ten years' residence in the Dominion, and no distinction is made between the man who came 
to this country possibly only a year before the war and the man who has been living here, as I said before, for twenty-five, thirty, forty, or fifty years, and who has proved his loyalty to the hilt. I am making no plea as to the man who is under any suspicion.
