The men for whom I speak have been residents in Canada for a long period, have all undergone the investigation of a judge, and been approved for citizenship, and I would draw the attention of the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) to his recognition of the justice of the claim of these people. I have already said this evening, and I am going to repeat the statement because the Prime Minister is now in his seat, that in the session of 1917 the leader of the Government stated that provision would be made whereby men of alien enemy origin who had long been resident in Canada and who could prove their loyalty-could prove that they were sympathetic to the Allies and so on-could be naturalized, and that Orders in Council .would be passed to that effect. Such Orders in Council were passed, and while practically no naturalizations were made under them, I think the mere fact that they were passed was a recognition that these men had a good case and should be considered. My suggestion is this:	If it is thought
right that men who came, we will say from Austria or Germany, or any other enemy country, perhaps a year or two before the war, may, after another ten years' residence in Canada be granted naturalization, surely the fact should count for something that other men have already lived here for twenty, or thirty years, and should not be placed on a par with those who have been here only a year or two. That seems to 'me eminently reasonable, and my suggestion is that cognizance should be taken of that fact. When I spoke before, I mentioned what the United States is doing in this connection, and I have a communication here which bears out my statement that the United States are not dealing in this way with their enemy aliens. That letter is from the Department of Labour to which had been referred a letter of mine addressed to the Department of State, and it reads as follows:
Washington, April 26, 1919.
The Department of State has referred to this department a copy of your letter of the 18th ultimo for response to the fourth inquiry therein.
Congress, by the Act of May 9, 1918 having made provision for the naturalization of enemy aliens, it would obviously be improper for any administrative officer of the Government to discourage their naturalization-

I may say this was in reply to my question as to whether there was any action on the part of the United States to discourage or forbid naturalization of people of alien enemy origin-
-nor has the department felt it a part of its duty actively to encourage their naturalization, believing that to be a matter within the discretion of the individual.
The United States Government is taking no such drastic action as is contemplated here. This is the new Act which has been passed by Congress and I shall read just a very small portion which says:
Section 11: No alien who is a native, citizen, subject, or denizen of any country, state or sovereignty with which the United States is at war shall he admitted to become a citizen ol the United States unless he made his declaration of intention not less than two nor more than seven years prior to the existence of the state of war, or was at that time entitled to become a citizen of the United States, without making a declaration of intention, or unless his petition for naturalization shall then be pending.
That is the case of some 93 residents of the constituency which I represent whose applications are now pending and upon which no action has been taken. The United States law. provides for applications which were pending.
-notwithstanding he shall be an alien enemj at the time and in the manner prescribed by the laws passed upon that subject.
Then follows this:
That the President of the United States may, in his discretion, upon investigation and report by the Department of Justice fully establishing the loyalty of any alien enemy not included in the foregoing exemption, except such alien enemy from the classification of alien enemies,
[DOT] and thereupon he shall have the privilege of applying for naturalization.
I am not making any plea for the man who cannot show that he is loyal or properly entitled to be a citizen or who has not conducted himself as a Canadian citizen should. I am asking this simply as a matter of justice to men who have lived in Canada for very many years, men of the class to which my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Pedlow) has already referred, men who have discharged their duties in every way, against whom there has never been a suspicion of disloyalty of any kind and some of whom have sons fighting in the war. It is unfair and un-British to deprive these men of the right of citizenship in a country which they have served so well. My amendment is as follows:
That paragraph (b) of subsection 4 of clause 8 be amended by adding the words:
"(4) Is the subject of a country which at the time of the passing of this Act was at war with His Majesty, provided that such subject was permanently resident in Canada on the fourth day of August, in the year one thousand nine hundred and nine."
That provides for ten years' residence in Canada at this time. If it is considered right that the men who have perhaps come from Germany or Austria only a few years ago and naturally would be more sympathetic to the country of their origin, should take ten years to become qualified to be Canadian citizens, then surely those who have lived here for thirty, forty and fifty years should be entitled to that privilege. Whereas the Solicitor General has stated that it is necessary to have our Act coincide with the British Act, I would point out to him that conditions in Canada are somewhat different from those in England. Conditions here are more similar to conditions prevailing in the United States. I present this amendment and I would like the members to give it that earnest consideration, to which I think it is entitled.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
I confess that the
amendment does not appear to be unreasonable, but as I would like to have an opportunity of considering whether or not it would be deemed a radical change from the provisions of the Imperial Act, and as there are several other elements in the proposal which I shall have to consider, I would ask that the matter stand over until some future occasion in order that I may have time to look into it.

subtopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AOT.
speechtext:
Section 8, paragraph B2, refers to a person who:
__is a member of a race or community known
to be opposed to the enemy Governments.
To what cases will that provision apply? Suppose an Alsatian or a person living in Lorraine had been naturalized before the war and since 1870; he belonged, by the Treaty of Versailles,, confirmed by the Treaty of Frankfurt, to Germany, but we all know that the Alsatian or the resident of Lorraine was not a German. In that case, would the Secretary of State consider that his naturalization should be revoked? Or, let us take the case af a Rumanian who was an inhabitant of Transylvania. Or, take the case of a Galician who was an Austrian subject, but whose race were practically living in a state of slavery and were very much opposed to the dominant power. You find a more complex case even in Macedonia, which is inhabited by Bulgarians, Serbians, Greeks and Armenians. There is

a medley of races under an enemy power. How can the Secretary of State arrive at a conclusion as regards the question whether or not naturalization papers should be revoked? It seems to me that this subsection is not broad enough, and perhaps my hon. friend, whilst considering the amendment of my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), might be a little more definite as regards the powers in connection with these races. To speak a little more broadly, I wish to refer to the Jewish race. We all know that the Jews are a self-assertive race. In spite of all the persecutions to which they have been subjected for many centuries, they have maintained the characteristics ,of their race. They go all over the world and become citizens of the world. The Jew is a Jew, and although his name may perhaps suggest enemy nationality, yet he is a Jew.
There are German Jews, Austrian Jews, Russian Jews; how will you distinguish between the Jew who is an enemy and the Jew who is not? Will you consider his adopted country-adopted by force of circumstances-as indicating the nationality which determines his citizenship? This is a very delicate subject. In the county of Gaspe there are large numbers of Jewish citizens; there are also many Jews in Maisonneuve. Many of these people came from enemy countries, but they are loyal citizens and it would be a great pity to debar them from British citizenship. If there is one thing that is to the credit of Great Britain and of British races generally, it is their generosity towards the Jewish race; in England we have had the best examples of that generosity in comparatively recent times. One of the great Prime Ministers of England, Disraeli, belonged to the great Jewish race; the great Chief Justice, Mr. Isaac, Lord Reading, also belongs to that race. 1 could name scores of others in Great Britain, in France and in the Allied countries who originally came from enemy countries and who, under these drastic powers vested in the Secretary of State, would be debarred from British citizenship. We have a large Jewish population in Canada which has come, in large numbers, from enemy countries; yet nobody would contend that they harbour any bad feelings toward our King, our Government, our constitution or our institutions. Under these circumstances, I ask my hon. friend to consider particularly the case of the Jews, whether they come from enemy countries or from friendly countries. During the war Great Britain and her Allies, especially 
France, have taken up the question of restoring Palestine to the Jewish race, and there is an international movement towards the settlement of Palestine by the repatriation of the children of Israel. The Government ought to be very careful not to antagonize the Jews and ought to see that they get the justice to which they are entitled.

speechtext: That is the trouble; you have general words like these-

speechtext: I simply want to point out that there is nothing in the Bill about Jews. We will let subsection (B) of section 8 stand and we will consider what has been said on these subjects. Sections 9 and 10 are merely formal sections and I suggest that they pass before the committee rises. There is a misprint in section 9; the words "Secretary of State of the United Kingdom" should be "Secretary of State having charge of the administration of the British Nationality and Status of Aliens Acts, 1914 and 1918, in the United Kingdom," and I move that the clause be so amended.
Amendment agreed to.

TME PRIME MINISTER'S BIRTHDAY.
speechtext: May I, on behalf of this House, offer my sincere congratulations to the right hon. the Prime Minister on the occasion of his birthday and wish him all success and prosperity.

subtopic: TME PRIME MINISTER'S BIRTHDAY.
speechtext: Many happy returns of the day.

subtopic: TME PRIME MINISTER'S BIRTHDAY.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TME PRIME MINISTER'S BIRTHDAY.
speechtext:
I am very grateful to my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) and to my hon. friends on both sides of the House for their congratulations and appreciation, although I must say that I have reached a stage in life when these anniversaries are not quite so welcome as they were some years ago.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden the House adjourned at 12, midnight.
